At the northern end of the parish, where the houses were scattered and people were scarce, Ingmar Ingmarsson stood alone on the bank, gazing out at the river. He was then almost sixty and looked even older. His face was weatherbeaten and furrowed, his figure bent. He appeared to be as awkward and helpless as ever. He stood leaning on a long, heavy boat hook, his dull, sleepy-looking eyes fixed on the water. The river raged and foamed, arrogantly marching past with all it had snatched from the lands above. Here and there you could see the floor of a house with some article of furniture still fastened to it. A chair or table would stand upright on the floor as it floated along, as if placed there by some unseen hand.

Ingmar Ingmarsson made no attempt to rescue any of the floating bridges or boat hulls that passed quite close to the bank. "All that will be seen to down at the village," he thought. Not for a second did his gaze wander from the river. He took note of everything that drifted past. All at once he spotted something bright and yellow floating on some loosely nailed boards quite a distance upriver. "Ah, this is what I have been expecting all along!" he said aloud. At first he could not quite make out what it was, but it looked as if some of those yellow birch-bark baskets in which children are rocked to sleep had been set on the boards.

It was not long before the peasant saw that he had guessed rightly. Now he could clearly see three little children in their yellow homespun frocks and round yellow hats, being carried downstream on a poorly built raft that was slowly being torn apart by the swift current and the moving ice floes.

The children were still a long way off. Big Ingmar knew there was a bend in the river where it touched his land. If God in His mercy would only direct the raft into this current, he thought, he might be able to get them ashore.

He stood very still, watching the raft. All at once it seemed as if someone had given it a push. It swung round and headed straight for the shore. By that time the children were so close he could see their frightened little faces and hear their cries. But they were still too far out to be reached by the boat hook from the bank. So he hurried down to the water's edge and waded into the river.
As he did so, he had a strange feeling that someone was calling him to come back. "You are no longer a young man, Ingmar. This may prove a dangerous business for you!" a voice said to him.

He thought a moment, wondering whether he had the right to risk his life. The wife whom he had once fetched from prison had died during the winter, and since her death his one longing had been that he might soon follow. But on the other hand, there was his son who needed a father's care, for he was only a little lad and could not look after the farm.
"In any case, it must be as God wills," he said.

Now Big Ingmar was no longer either awkward or slow. As he plunged into the raging river, he planted his boat hook firmly in the bottom so as not to be carried away by the current. He took good care to dodge the floating ice and driftwood. When the raft with the children was quite near, he pressed his feet down into the riverbed, thrust out his boat hook, and got a grip on it.

"Hold on tight!" he shouted to the children, for just then the raft made a sudden turn and all its planks creaked. But the wretched structure held together, and Big Ingmar managed to pull it out of the strongest current. That done, he let go of it, for he knew the raft would now drift shoreward by itself.

Touching bottom with his boat hook again, he turned to go back to the bank. This time, however, he failed to notice a huge log rushing toward him. It caught him in the side just below the armpit. It was a terrific blow, for the log was hurled against him with a force that sent him staggering in the water. Yet he kept a tight grip on the boat hook until he reached the bank. When he again stood on firm ground, he hardly dared touch his body, for he felt that his chest had been crushed. "I have received my death blow," he said calmly, and walked slowly home.

The pastor was called in and remained at the Ingmar Farm the whole afternoon. On his way home, he stopped at the schoolmaster's. He had experienced things in the course of the day that he felt the need of telling to someone who would understand.

Storm and Mother Stina were deeply grieved, for they had already heard that Ingmar Ingmarsson was dead. The clergyman, on the other hand, looked almost radiant as he stepped into the schoolmaster's kitchen.
Storm immediately asked the pastor if he had been in time.
"Yes," he said, "but on this occasion I was not needed."
"Weren't you?" said Mother Stina.
"No," answered the pastor with a mysterious smile. "He would have gotten on just as well without me. Sometimes it is very hard to sit by a deathbed," he added.
"It is indeed," nodded the schoolmaster.
"Particularly when the one who is passing from among us happens to be the best man in your parish."
"Just so."
"But things can also be quite different from what one had imagined."
For a moment the pastor sat quietly gazing into space. His eyes looked clearer than usual behind the spectacles.
"Have you, Storm, or you, Mother Stina, ever heard of the wonderful thing that once happened to Big Ingmar when he was a young man?" he asked.
The schoolmaster said he had heard many wonderful things about him.

"Why, of course. But this is the most wonderful of all! I never knew of it myself until today. Big Ingmar had a good friend who has always lived in a little cabin on his estate," the pastor continued.
"Yes, I know," said the schoolmaster. "He is also named Ingmar. Folks call him Strong Ingmar, to tell them apart."

"True," said the pastor. "His father named him Ingmar in honor of the master's family. One Saturday evening at midsummer, when the nights are almost as light as the days, Big Ingmar and his friend Strong Ingmar finished their work, put on their Sunday clothes, and went down to the village looking for amusement."

The pastor paused for a moment, thinking it over. “I can imagine the night must have been beautiful,” he went on, “clear and still — one of those nights when earth and sky seem to trade colors, the sky turning a bright green while the earth veils itself in white mist, giving everything a bluish-white tinge. When Big Ingmar and Strong Ingmar were crossing the bridge into the village, it was as if someone had told them to stop and look up. So they did. And they saw heaven open! The whole sky had been drawn back to left and right, like a pair of curtains, and the two of them stood there, hand in hand, and saw all the glories of heaven. Have you ever heard anything like it, Mother Stina, or you, Storm?” the pastor said in an awed voice. “Just imagine those two standing on the bridge, watching heaven open! But they never told a soul what they saw. Now and then they might tell a child or a relative that they’d once seen heaven open, but they never spoke of it to outsiders. Still, the vision lived on in their memory as their greatest treasure, their holy of holies.”

The pastor closed his eyes for a moment and heaved a deep sigh. "I have never before heard of such things." His voice shook a little as he continued. "I only wish I had stood on the bridge with Big Ingmar and Strong Ingmar and seen heaven open!"

"This morning, immediately after Big Ingmar had been carried home, he asked that Strong Ingmar be sent for. A messenger was dispatched to the croft at once to fetch him, only to find that Strong Ingmar was not at home. He was in the forest somewhere, chopping firewood, and was not easy to find. Messenger after messenger went in search of him. In the meantime, Big Ingmar felt very anxious, fearing he might not get to see his old friend again in this life. First the doctor came, then I came, but still no Strong Ingmar. Big Ingmar suffered greatly and took no notice of the rest of us. Only the children could comfort him. Whenever the pain became too much, he would call the children to him. He has two—a boy named Ingmar, who is about four, and a girl named Brita, who is about six. He would take the little ones in his arms and hold them fast, and whenever he felt a sharp pang he would press them to his heart. But the moment it passed, he let them go."

"At last they found the crofter. Big Ingmar glanced away from the children with a sigh of relief when he heard Strong Ingmar's heavy step in the hallway. When his friend came over to the bedside, he took his hand and patted it gently, saying: 'Do you remember the time when you and I stood on the bridge and saw heaven open?' 'As if I could ever forget that night when we two had a vision of Paradise!' Strong Ingmar responded. Then Big Ingmar turned toward him, his face beaming with joy, and said: 'Today you and I shall go on a pilgrimage together.' Those were his last words. A moment later he was dead."
The schoolmaster and his wife thought, with the pastor, that it was a beautiful death. All three of them sat profoundly silent for a long while.
"But what could Strong Ingmar have meant," asked Mother Stina suddenly, "when he spoke of the pilgrimage?"

The pastor looked up, somewhat perplexed. "I don't know," he replied. "Big Ingmar died just after that was said, and I have not had time to ponder it." He fell to thinking, then spoke half to himself: "It was a strange sort of thing to say. You're right about that, Mother Stina."
"You know, of course, that it has been said of Strong Ingmar that he can see into the future?" she said thoughtfully.

The pastor sat stroking his forehead in an effort to collect his thoughts. "The ways of Providence cannot be reasoned out by the finite mind," he mused. "I cannot fathom them. Yet seeking to know them is the most satisfying thing in all the world."

chapters.title: Book Two — Karin, Daughter Of Ingmar
paragraphs: Autumn had come, and school was open again. One morning, during the children's recess, the schoolmaster and Gertrude went into the kitchen and sat down at the table, where Mother Stina served them coffee. Before they'd finished their cups, a visitor arrived.

The caller was a young peasant named Halvor Halvorsson, who'd recently opened a shop in the village. He came from Tims Farm and was known familiarly as Tims Halvor — a tall, good-looking fellow who seemed somewhat down in the dumps. Mother Stina asked him to join them for coffee too, so he sat down at the table, poured himself a cup, and started talking to the schoolmaster.

Mother Stina sat knitting by the window, from where she could see down the road. All at once she flushed and leaned forward for a better look. Trying to sound unconcerned, she said, with feigned indifference, "The grand folk seem to be out walking today."
Tims Halvor thought he caught something peculiar in her tone, and he got up to look out for himself. He saw a tall, stoop-shouldered woman and a half-grown boy coming toward the schoolhouse.
"Unless my eyes deceive me, that's Karin, daughter of Ingmar!" said Mother Stina.

"It's Karin, all right," Tims Halvor confirmed. He said nothing more, but turned away from the window and glanced around the room as though looking for some way to escape. After a moment, though, he quietly went back to his seat.

The summer before, while Big Ingmar was still alive, Halvor had courted Karin Ingmarsson. It had been a long courtship, with a good many ifs and buts on her family's side — the old Ingmars weren't entirely sure he was good enough for Karin. It wasn't a matter of money, since Halvor was well-off; but his father had been a drinker, and who was to say the failing hadn't passed down to the son? In the end, though, it was decided that Halvor should have Karin. The wedding day was set, and they'd asked to have the banns read. But before the date fixed for the first reading, Karin and Halvor traveled to Falun to buy the wedding ring and the prayer book. They were gone three days, and when they got back, Karin told her father she couldn't marry Halvor after all. She had nothing against him, she said, except that once he'd had a drop too much, and she was afraid he might turn out like his father. Big Ingmar told her he wouldn't try to talk her out of her own better judgment, so Halvor was sent away, and the engagement was off.

Halvor took it very much to heart. "You're heaping shame on me that will be hard to bear," he said. "What will people think, you throwing me over like this? It isn't fair to treat a decent man that way."

But Karin wouldn't be moved, and ever since, Halvor had been sullen and unhappy. He couldn't forget the wrong the Ingmarssons had done him. And now here sat Halvor, and here came Karin! What would happen next? One thing was certain — any reconciliation was out of the question. Since the autumn before, Karin had been married to a man named Elof Ersson. She and her husband lived at the Ingmar Farm, which they'd been running since Big Ingmar died that spring. Big Ingmar had left five daughters and one son, but the son was still too young to take over the property.

By now Karin had come in. She was only about twenty-two, but she was one of those women who never look quite young. Most people thought her plain — she took after her father's side, with their heavy eyelids, sandy hair, and hard lines around the mouth. But the schoolmaster and his wife were pleased that she resembled the old Ingmars so strongly. When Karin saw Halvor, her expression didn't change. She moved around slowly and quietly, greeting each of them in turn; when she held out her hand to Halvor, he put out his, and they barely brushed fingertips. Karin always stooped a little, and standing before Halvor now, head bowed, she seemed even more bent than usual, while Halvor looked taller and straighter than ever.
"So Karin's really ventured out today?" said Mother Stina, pulling up the pastor's chair for her.
"Yes," she answered. "It's easy walking now that the frost has set in."
"There was a hard frost last night," the schoolmaster put in.
A dead silence followed, lasting several minutes. Presently Halvor got to his feet, and the others gave a start, as though suddenly woken from a deep sleep.
"I must get back to the shop," said Halvor.
"What's the hurry?" asked Mother Stina.
"I hope Halvor isn't leaving on my account," Karin said meekly.

The moment Halvor was gone, the tension broke, and the schoolmaster knew at once what to say. He looked over at the boy Karin had brought with her, whom no one had paid any attention to until now. He was a small lad, probably not much older than Gertrude, with a fair, soft baby face — yet there was something about him that made him seem old for his years. It was easy to tell what family he belonged to.
"I think Karin's brought us a new pupil," said Storm.
"This is my brother," Karin replied. "He's the present Ingmar Ingmarsson."
"He's rather small for that name," Storm remarked.
"Yes — father died too soon!"
"He did indeed," the schoolmaster and his wife said, both in the same breath.
"He's been going to school in Falun," Karin explained. "That's why he hasn't been here before."
"Aren't you sending him back this year too?"
Karin lowered her eyes, and a sigh escaped her. "He's got the name of being a good student," she said, sidestepping the question.
"I'm only afraid I won't be able to teach him a thing. He must already know as much as I do."

"Well, I expect the schoolmaster knows a good deal more than a little chap like him." Then came another pause, after which Karin went on: "It's not only a question of him attending school here. I'd also like to ask whether you and Mother Stina would let the boy come and live with you."
The schoolmaster and his wife looked at each other in astonishment, and neither was ready with an answer.
"I'm afraid our quarters are rather cramped," Storm said after a moment.
"I thought perhaps you'd be willing to take milk and butter and eggs as part of the payment."
"As to that—"
"You'd be doing me a great service," said the well-off farmer's wife.
Mother Stina sensed that Karin would never have made such an unusual request without some good reason behind it, so she settled the matter at once.
"Karin need say no more. We'll do everything we can for the Ingmarssons."
"Thank you," said Karin.

The two women went on discussing what would be best for Ingmar's welfare. Meanwhile Storm took the boy off to the classroom and sat him down next to Gertrude. Through the whole of that first day, Ingmar never said a word.

Tims Halvor didn't go near the schoolhouse again for a week or more — as if he were afraid of running into Karin there again. But one morning, when the rain was coming down in torrents and no customers were likely to show up, he decided to run over and have a chat with Mother Stina. He was hungry for a heart-to-heart talk with someone kind and sympathetic. A terrible fit of the blues had taken hold of him. "I'm no good, and nobody respects me," he muttered, tormenting himself the way he'd been in the habit of doing ever since Karin had thrown him over.

He closed up the shop, buttoned his storm coat, and made his way to the school through wind and rain and slush. Halvor was glad to be back in the friendly atmosphere of the schoolhouse, and he was still there when the recess bell rang and Storm and the two children came in for their coffee. All three came over to greet him. He got up to shake hands with the schoolmaster, but when little Ingmar put out his hand, Halvor was talking so earnestly to Mother Stina that he seemed not to notice the boy at all. Ingmar stood there a moment, then went and sat down at the table. He sighed several times, just as Karin had done the day she was there.
"Halvor's come to show us his new watch," said Mother Stina.

Halvor took a new silver watch out of his pocket and showed it around. It was a pretty little thing, with a flower design engraved on the case. The schoolmaster opened it up, went into the schoolroom for a magnifying glass, fitted it to his eye, and set about examining the works. He seemed thoroughly absorbed studying the delicate arrangement of the tiny wheels, and said he'd never seen finer workmanship. Finally he handed the watch back to Halvor, who pocketed it looking neither pleased nor proud — not the way people usually look when their purchase is being praised.
Ingmar stayed quiet through the meal, but once he'd finished his coffee, he asked Storm whether he really knew anything about watches.
"Why, of course," the schoolmaster replied. "Don't you know I understand a little of everything?"

Then Ingmar brought out a watch he carried in his vest pocket. It was a big, round silver turnip of a watch, ugly and clumsy next to Halvor's, with a chain that was just as clumsy a contraption. The case was plain and dented — not much of a watch at all. It had no crystal, and the enamel on its face was cracked.
"It's stopped," said Storm, holding the watch to his ear.
"Yes, I kn-n-know," the boy stammered. "I was just wondering if you didn't think it could be fixed."
Storm opened it up and found all the wheels loose. "You must have been driving nails with this thing," he said. "There's nothing I can do with it."
"Don't you think Eric the clockmaker could fix it?"
"No, no better than I could. You'd best send it to Falun and have a whole new set of works put in."
"That's what I thought," said Ingmar, and took the watch back.
"For heaven's sake, what have you been doing with it?" the schoolmaster exclaimed.
The boy swallowed hard. "It was father's watch," he explained, "and it got smashed like that when father was hit by the whirling log."
Now everyone's interest was caught.

Struggling to keep his composure, Ingmar went on: "As you know, it happened during Holy Week, when I was home. I was the first one to reach father when he was lying on the riverbank. I found him with the watch in his hand. 'It's all over with me now, Ingmar,' he said. 'I'm sorry the watch is broken, because I want you to give it, with my regards, to someone I've wronged.' Then he told me who was to have it, and told me to take it to Falun and have it repaired before I gave it over. But I never made it back to Falun, and now I don't know what to do about it."
The schoolmaster was wondering whether he knew of anyone headed to the city soon, when Mother Stina turned to the boy:
"Who was the watch meant for, Ingmar?" she asked.
"I don't know that I ought to say," the boy hedged.
"Wasn't it Tims Halvor, sitting right here?"
"Yes," he whispered.
"Then give Halvor the watch just as it is," said Mother Stina. "That will please him most."
Ingmar obediently got up, took out the watch, and rubbed it against his coat sleeve to shine it up a little. Then he went over to Halvor.
"Father asked me to give you this, with his compliments," he said, holding out the watch.

All this while Halvor had sat there silent and glum. When the boy came over to him, he put a hand up over his eyes, as though he didn't want to look at him. Ingmar stood there a long time holding out the watch, until finally he cast an appealing glance at Mother Stina.
"Blessed are the peacemakers," she said.

Then Storm put in a word of his own. "I don't think you could ask for a better amends than this, Halvor," he said. "I've always maintained that if Ingmar Ingmarsson had lived, he'd have given you full justice long before now."
The next thing anyone saw was Halvor reaching for the watch, almost as if against his own will. But the instant it was in his hand, he tucked it into the inside pocket of his vest.
"No fear of anyone taking that watch off him now," the schoolmaster said with a laugh, watching Halvor carefully button his coat.
Halvor laughed too. After a moment he stood up, straightened his shoulders, and drew a deep breath. Color rose in his cheeks, and his eyes shone with a new, unexpected happiness.
"Now Halvor must feel like a new man," said the schoolmaster's wife.

Then Halvor reached inside his overcoat and pulled out his own brand-new watch. Crossing over to Ingmar, who'd sat back down at the table, he said, "Since I've taken your father's watch from you, you must take this one from me."

He laid the watch on the table and walked out without even saying goodbye. He spent the rest of the day tramping the roads and back lanes. A couple of farmers who'd come some distance to do business with him hung around outside the shop from noon until evening. But Tims Halvor never showed up.

Elof Ersson, Karin Ingmarsson's husband, was the son of a cruel and grasping peasant who'd always treated him harshly. As a child he'd been half starved, and even once he was grown, his father kept him under his thumb. He had to work himself to the bone from morning to night and was never allowed any pleasures — he wasn't even permitted to go to the country dances like other young people, and he got no rest from his labor even on Sundays. Marrying didn't make Elof his own master either. He had to live at the Ingmar Farm under his father-in-law's rule, and there too hard work and frugality were the order of the day. As long as Ingmar Ingmarsson was alive, Elof seemed perfectly content with his lot, laboring away without so much as a word of complaint. People used to say the Ingmarssons had finally gotten a son-in-law after their own hearts, since Elof Ersson didn't seem to know that there was anything to life besides toil and drudgery.

But the moment Big Ingmar was dead and buried, Elof took up drinking and carousing. He fell in with every ne'er-do-well in the parish, invited them down to the farm, and went off with them to dance halls and taverns. He gave up work entirely and drank himself senseless every day. Within two short months he'd become a wretched drunkard.

The first time Karin saw him drunk, she was horrified. This is God's judgment on me for how I treated Halvor, was the thought that came to her. She said very little to her husband by way of rebuke or warning. She soon saw that he was like a blighted tree, doomed to wither and rot, and that she could hope for neither help nor protection from him.

But Karin's sisters weren't as wise as she was. They resented his escapades, blushed at his crude songs and coarse jokes, and alternated between threatening him and scolding him. Their brother-in-law was good-natured enough on the whole, but sometimes he flew into a rage and had words with them. Then Karin's only thought was how to get her sisters out of the house, so they could escape the misery she herself had to live in. Over the course of the summer she managed to marry off the two older girls, and sent the two younger ones to America, where they had well-off relatives.

Each sister received her share of the inheritance, which came to twenty thousand kronor apiece. The farm itself had been left to Karin, with the understanding that young Ingmar would take it over once he came of age.

It seemed remarkable that Karin, who was so awkward and diffident, had managed to send so many birds from the nest, finding mates and homes for every one of them. She'd arranged it all herself, since she could get no help at all from her husband, who by now was utterly worthless.

Her greatest worry, though, was the little brother — the boy who was now Ingmar Ingmarsson. He exasperated Karin's husband even more than the sisters had. He did it through actions rather than words: once he poured out all the corn brandy Elof had brought home; another time his brother-in-law caught him watering down his liquor.
When autumn came, Karin insisted the boy be sent back to school that year, as in years past, but her husband, who was also his guardian, wouldn't hear of it.

"Ingmar's going to be a farmer, like his father and me and my father before me," said Elof. "What business does he have at school? When winter comes, he and I are going into the forest to set up charcoal kilns. That'll be the best schooling he could get. When I was his age I spent a whole winter working the kiln."
Since Karin couldn't talk him out of it, she had to make the best of things and keep Ingmar at home for the time being.

Elof then tried to win little Ingmar's trust. Whenever he went anywhere, he always wanted the boy along. The boy went, of course, but unwillingly — he had no wish to accompany him on his drinking bouts. So Elof would coax him, swearing he wasn't going any farther than the church or the shop. But once he had Ingmar in the cart, he'd drive off with him down to the smithies at Bergsana, or the tavern at Karmsund.
Karin was glad her husband took the boy along; it was at least some safeguard against Elof being left lying in a ditch by the roadside, or driving the horse to death.
Once, when Elof came home at eight in the morning, Ingmar was sitting beside him in the cart, fast asleep.
"Come out here and see to the boy!" Elof shouted to Karin. "Carry him in — the poor brat's full as a tick and can't walk a step."

Karin was so shocked she nearly collapsed. She had to sit down on the steps a moment to steady herself before she could lift the boy. The instant she took hold of him, she realized he wasn't really asleep, but stiff with cold and unconscious. She carried him in her arms into the bedroom, locked the door behind her, and tried to bring him around. After a while she went into the living room, where Elof sat eating his breakfast. She walked straight up to him and put her hand on his shoulder.

"You'd better eat a good meal while you're at it," she said, "because if you've made my brother drink himself to death, you'll soon be putting up with poorer fare than you get here on the Ingmar Farm."
"Listen to you! As if a little brandy could hurt him!"
"Mark my words. If the boy dies, you'll get twenty years in prison, Elof."
When Karin went back into the bedroom, the boy had come out of his stupor, but he was delirious now, unable to move a hand or a foot. He was in agony.
"Do you think I'm going to die, Karin?" he moaned.
"No, dear, of course not," Karin assured him.
"I didn't know what they were giving me."
"Thank God for that," said Karin fervently.
"If I die, write to my sisters and tell them I didn't know it was liquor," the boy wailed.
"Yes, dear," Karin soothed him.
"Really and truly, I didn't know — I swear it!"
All day Ingmar lay in a raging fever. "Please don't tell father about it!" he raved.
"Father will never know of it," she said.
"But suppose I die — then father's bound to find out, and I'll be shamed before him."
"But it wasn't your fault, child."

"Maybe father will think I shouldn't have taken what Elof gave me. Don't you suppose the whole parish already knows I was drunk?" he asked. "What are the hired men saying, and old Lisa, and Strong Ingmar?"
"They're not saying anything," Karin replied.

"You'll have to tell them exactly how it happened. We were at the tavern in Karmsund, where Elof and some of his friends had been drinking all night long. I was sitting in a corner on a bench, half asleep, when Elof came over and shook me awake. 'Wake up, Ingmar,' he said, very friendly-like, 'and I'll give you something to warm you up. Drink this,' he said, holding a glass to my lips. 'It's only hot water with a bit of sugar in it.' I was shivering with cold when I woke, and as I drank it I only noticed that it was hot and sweet. But he'd gone and mixed something strong into it! Oh, what will father say?"
Then Karin opened the door to the living room, where Elof was still lingering over his meal. She thought it would do him good to hear this.
"If only father were alive, Karin — if only father were still alive!"
"What then, Ingmar?"
"Don't you think he'd kill him?"
Elof burst into loud laughter, and when the boy heard it, he went so pale with fright that Karin quickly shut the door again.
It did have one good effect on Elof, at least — he raised no objection when Karin decided to send the boy to Storm's school.

Soon after Halvor got the watch, his shop was always full of people. Every farmer in the parish, whenever he was in town, would stop by Halvor's shop to hear the story of Big Ingmar's watch. The peasants, in their long white fur coats, would lean over the counter by the hour, their solemn, weathered faces turned toward Halvor as he talked. Sometimes he'd take the watch out and show them the dented case and the cracked face.

"So that's where the blow caught him," the peasants would say, and they seemed to picture right before them what had happened when Big Ingmar was hurt. "It's a great thing for you, Halvor, to have that watch."
Whenever Halvor showed the watch around, he never let it out of his hands — he always kept a tight grip on the chain.

One day Halvor stood talking to a group of farmers, telling them the usual story, and at the climax the watch was of course brought out. As it passed from hand to hand — Halvor still holding the chain — a solemn hush fell over everyone. Meanwhile Elof had come into the shop, but since everyone's attention was fixed on the watch, no one had noticed him come in. Elof had heard the story of his father-in-law's watch too, and knew right away what was going on. He didn't begrudge Halvor his keepsake; he just found it funny, the sight of him and all the others standing there so solemn over nothing but a battered old silver watch.

Elof crept quietly up behind the men, reached over, and snatched the watch away from Halvor. It was only meant as a joke — he had no intention of actually taking it from him, he just wanted to tease him a little.

When Halvor tried to grab it back, Elof stepped away and held it up, the way you'd dangle a lump of sugar in front of a dog. Then Halvor vaulted the counter, and he looked so furious that Elof got scared — instead of standing still and handing the watch back, he made a run for the door.
Outside were some badly worn wooden steps; Elof's foot caught in a hole and down he went. Halvor fell on him, grabbed the watch back, then gave him several hard kicks.
"You'd better quit kicking me and see what's wrong with my back," said Elof.
Halvor stopped at once, but Elof made no move to get up.
"Help me up," he said.
"You can help yourself once you've slept off your bender."
"I'm not drunk," Elof protested. "The truth is, as I started down the steps I thought I saw Big Ingmar coming toward me to take the watch back. That's how I took such a bad fall."

Then Halvor bent down and helped the poor wretch up — his back was broken. He had to be loaded into a wagon and driven home. He would never have the use of his legs again. From then on Elof was confined to his bed, a helpless cripple. But he could still talk, and all day long he kept begging for brandy. The doctor had left strict orders with Karin not to give him any spirits, for fear he'd drink himself to death. So Elof tried to get what he wanted by shrieking and making the most horrible noises, especially at night. He carried on like a madman and kept everyone from getting any rest.

That was Karin's hardest year. Her husband sometimes tormented her until it seemed she couldn't bear it a moment longer. The very air was poisoned by his foul talk and cursing, until the house was like a hell. Karin begged the Storms to keep little Ingmar with them during the holidays too; she didn't want her brother home with her for even a single day, not even at Christmas.

All the servants at the Ingmar Farm were distant relations of the family and had always lived on the place. If not for their sense of belonging to the Ingmarssons, they never could have gone on working under such conditions. There were precious few nights they were allowed to sleep undisturbed. Elof was forever coming up with new ways to torment both the servants and Karin, trying to force them into giving him what he wanted.
In this misery Karin passed a winter, a summer, and another winter.

But Karin had one refuge she'd flee to at times, to be alone with her thoughts. Behind the hop garden there was a narrow bench where she often sat, elbows on her knees and chin resting in her hands, staring straight ahead and seeing nothing at all. Before her stretched great fields of grain, and beyond them the forest, and in the far distance the range of hills and Mount Klack.

One evening in April she sat on her bench, feeling tired and listless, the way one often does in springtime, when the snow's turning to slush and the ground hasn't yet been washed clean by the spring rains. The hops lay sleeping under a covering of fir branches. Against the hills hung the thick mist that always comes with a thaw. The birch tops were just starting to turn brown, but along the edge of the forest there was still a deep border of snow. Real spring would soon be here, and the thought of it only made her feel more tired. She felt she could never live through another summer like the last one. She thought of all the work ahead of her — sowing and haymaking, spring baking and spring cleaning, weaving and sewing — and wondered how she'd ever get through it all.
"I might as well be dead," she sighed. "I seem to be here for no other reason than to keep Elof from drinking himself to death."

Suddenly she looked up, as though she'd heard someone call her name. Leaning against the hedge, looking straight at her, stood Halvor Halvorsson. She had no idea when he'd arrived, but he'd apparently been standing there a good while.
"I thought I'd find you over here," Halvor said.
"Oh, did you?"
"I remembered how, back in the old days, you used to slip away and come sit here and brood."
"I didn't have much to brood over back then."
"Then your troubles were mostly imaginary."

Karin thought to herself as she looked at Halvor: He must be thinking what a fool I was, not marrying a man so handsome and dignified. Now he's got me right where he can crow over me, and he's only come to laugh.
"I've been inside talking with Elof," Halvor explained. "He's really who I came to see."
Karin made no reply, just sat there cold and unresponsive, eyes fixed on the ground, hands folded, bracing herself for all the scorn she imagined Halvor was about to heap on her.

"I told him," Halvor went on, "that I considered myself largely to blame for what happened to him, since it was at my place he got hurt." He paused a moment, as though waiting for some reaction from her, approval or disapproval. But Karin said nothing. "So I've asked him to come and stay with me a while. It would at least be a change, and he'd see more people there than he does here."
Karin raised her eyes then, but otherwise stayed as still as before.

"We've arranged to have him sent to my place tomorrow morning. I know he'll come, because he thinks he'll get his liquor there. But of course you know, Karin, that's out of the question. No indeed — he'll get no more of it from me than he does from you. I'll expect him tomorrow. He's to have the little room off the shop, and I've promised him I'll leave his door standing open, so he can see everyone who comes and goes."
At Halvor's first words Karin wondered whether he'd made the whole thing up, but little by little it dawned on her that he meant every word.

The truth was, Karin had always assumed Halvor had courted her only for her money and her good family connections. It had never once occurred to her that he might have loved her for herself. She probably knew she wasn't the sort of girl men fell for. Nor had she herself ever been in love, not with Halvor and not with Elof. But now that Halvor had come to her in her trouble, wanting to help, she was completely overwhelmed by the largeness of the man. She marveled that he could be so kind. Surely, she felt, he must like her at least a little, to come to her like this.

Karin's heart began pounding, violent and anxious. She was waking to something she'd never felt before, and wondered what it meant. Then all at once she understood: Halvor's kindness had thawed her frozen heart, and love was starting to flare up in her. Halvor went on laying out his plan, worried the whole time that she might object. "It's hard on Elof too," he pleaded. "He needs a change of scene, and he won't give me as much trouble as he's given you. It'll be different once he's got a man to answer to."
Karin hardly knew what to do. She felt she couldn't move or say a word without letting Halvor see she was in love with him, and yet she knew she'd have to give him some kind of answer.
After a while Halvor stopped talking and simply looked at her.
Then Karin rose, and almost without meaning to, went up to him and patted his hand. "God bless you, Halvor," she said, her voice breaking. "God bless you."
For all her care, Halvor must have sensed something, because he quickly caught her hands and drew her toward him.
"No! No!" she cried in alarm, pulling free; then she hurried away.
Elof had gone to live with Halvor. All summer he lay in the little bedroom off the shop. Halvor wasn't burdened with caring for him for very long, though, because he died that autumn.
Shortly after his death, Mother Stina said to Halvor, "Now you must promise me one thing — promise me you'll be patient where Karin's concerned."
"Of course I'll be patient," Halvor answered, puzzled.
"She's someone worth winning, even if it takes seven long years."
But patience wasn't so easy for Halvor, because he soon learned that this man and that one were paying court to Karin. It started within two weeks of Elof's funeral.

One Sunday afternoon Halvor sat on the steps in front of his shop, watching people come and go. It struck him presently that an unusual number of fine rigs were heading toward the Ingmar Farm. In the first carriage sat an inspector from Bergsana Foundry, in the second the son of the man who ran the Karmsund Inn, and last of all came Magistrate Berger Sven Persson, the richest man in western Dalecarlia, and a sensible, highly respected one too. He wasn't young, to be sure — he'd been married twice already, and was now a widower for the second time.

When Halvor saw Berger Sven Persson drive past, he couldn't hold himself back any longer. He jumped to his feet and set off down the road; in almost no time he was across the bridge and on the side of the river where the Ingmar Farm stood.

"I'd like to know where all those carriages ended up," he told himself. He followed the wheel ruts, half running, growing more determined with every step. "I know this is foolish of me," he thought, remembering Mother Stina's warning. "But I'm only going as far as the gate, just to see what they're up to down there."

In the best room at the Ingmar farmhouse sat Berger Sven Persson and two other men, drinking coffee. Ingmar Ingmarsson, who was still living at the schoolhouse, was home for the Sunday. He sat at the table with them, acting as host, since Karin had excused herself, saying she had work to do in the kitchen — the maids had gone down to the mission house to hear the schoolmaster preach.

It was deadly dull in the parlor. The men sat drinking their coffee without a word passing between them. The suitors were practically strangers to each other, and all three were watching for a chance to slip into the kitchen for a private word with Karin.
Presently the door opened and another caller stepped in, greeted by Ingmar and shown to the table.
"This is Tims Halvor Halvorsson," said Ingmar, introducing the newcomer to Berger Sven Persson.
Sven Persson didn't get up, just greeted Halvor with a sweep of his hand, saying, rather mockingly:
"A pleasure to meet so distinguished a personage."
Ingmar noisily pulled up a chair for Halvor, sparing him the awkwardness of having to reply.

From the moment Halvor walked in, all the suitors turned chatty and started talking big. Each one took a turn praising and championing the others — as if they'd all silently agreed to stick together until Halvor was safely out of the running.
"The magistrate's driving a fine horse today," the inspector began.

Berger Sven Persson joined in the game by complimenting the inspector on the bear he'd shot the winter before. Then the two of them turned to the innkeeper's son and said something in praise of a house his father was building.

Finally all three of them went on about the wealth of Berger Sven Persson. They grew quite eloquent, and with every word they made it plain to Halvor that he was too lowly a man to even think of matching himself against them. And Halvor certainly did feel very small, and bitterly regretted having come.

Just then Karin came in with fresh coffee. At the sight of Halvor she brightened for a moment, but then it struck her that his calling on her so soon after her husband's death looked rather bad. If he's in such a hurry, she thought, people will say he didn't take proper care of Elof, and that he wanted him out of the way so he could marry me. She wished he'd waited two or three years before coming — that would have been long enough for people to see he hadn't been impatient for Elof to be gone. Why does he have to be in such a rush? she wondered. Surely he must know I don't want anyone but him.

Everyone had stopped talking the moment Karin appeared, curious to see how she and Halvor would greet each other. They barely touched hands. At this the magistrate expressed his delight with a short whistle, while the inspector burst into a loud guffaw. Halvor turned to him quietly. "What are you laughing at?" he said.
The inspector was at a loss for an answer. With Karin standing there, he didn't want to say anything that might give offense.
"He's thinking of a hound that flushes the hare and lets somebody else catch it," the innkeeper's son remarked slyly.

Karin turned blood red, but went on refilling the coffee cups. "Berger Sven Persson and the rest of you will have to make do with plain coffee," she said. "We no longer serve spirits to anyone on this farm."
"Nor do I, at my house," said the magistrate approvingly.
The inspector and the innkeeper's son fell silent; they understood that Sven Persson had scored a real point.

The magistrate promptly launched into a discourse on temperance and its wholesome effects. Karin listened with interest and agreed with everything he said. Seeing that this was the kind of talk that appealed to her, the magistrate warmed to his subject and delivered a long-winded speech on the curse of liquor and drunkenness. Karin recognized all her own thoughts on the matter in what he said, and was glad to find them shared by so intelligent a man as the magistrate.
In the middle of his monologue, Berger Sven Persson glanced over at Halvor, who sat at the table looking glum and sulky, his coffee cup untouched.

It's rather rough on him, Berger Sven Persson thought, especially if there's any truth to what people say about his giving Elof a little help on his way out of this world. Still, he did Karin a good service, ridding her of that dreadful drunkard. And since the magistrate figured he'd as good as won the game by now, he felt rather warmly toward Halvor. Raising his cup, he said, "Here's to you, Halvor. You certainly did Karin a good turn, taking that drunken sot of a husband off her hands."
Halvor didn't respond to the toast. He sat there looking the man straight in the eye, trying to decide how to take it.
The inspector burst out laughing again. "Yes, yes, a good turn," he haw-hawed, "a real good turn."
"Yes, yes, a real good turn," echoed the innkeeper's son, chuckling.

Before they'd finished laughing, Karin had slipped out through the kitchen door like a shadow — but from the kitchen she could still hear everything said inside. She felt both sorry and troubled over Halvor's ill-timed visit. It would probably mean she could never marry him now. It was clear the gossips were already spreading ugly rumors. "I can't bear the thought of losing him," she sighed.
For a while no sound came from the sitting room, but then she heard a noise like a chair being pushed back. Someone had evidently gotten up.
"Are you leaving already, Halvor?" she heard young Ingmar say.
"Yes," Halvor replied. "I can't stay any longer. Please say goodbye to Karin for me."
"Why don't you go into the kitchen and say it yourself?"
"No," she heard Halvor answer, "the two of us have nothing more to say to each other."

Karin's heart began pounding, and thoughts came rushing into her head as if on wings. Now Halvor was angry with her — and no wonder. She'd hardly even dared to shake his hand, and when the others mocked him, she never said a word in his defense, just slipped quietly away. Now he must think she didn't care for him, and so he was leaving, never to come back. She couldn't understand why she'd treated him so shabbily, she who cared for him so much. Then, all at once, her father's old saying came back to her: The Ingmarssons need fear no man; they need only walk in the ways of God.
Karin quickly opened the door and stood facing Halvor before he could manage to leave the room.
"Are you leaving so soon, Halvor?" she asked. "I thought you'd be staying for supper."
Halvor stood there staring at Karin. She seemed utterly changed — her cheeks glowed, and there was something tender and appealing about her he'd never seen before.
"I'm going, and I'm not coming back," said Halvor, apparently missing her meaning.

"Do stay and finish your coffee," she urged. Then she took him by the hand and led him back to the table. She went white, then red, and more than once nearly lost her nerve entirely. But she pushed through it, though there was nothing on earth she feared more than scorn and contempt. At least now he'll see that I'm willing to stand by him, she thought. Turning to her guests, she said, "Berger Sven Persson, and all the rest of you — Halvor and I haven't spoken of this, since I've only so recently become a widow. But it seems best now that you all know I'd rather marry Halvor than anyone else in the world." She paused to steady her voice, then finished: "Say what you like about it, but Halvor and I have done nothing wrong."
When Karin had finished speaking, she moved closer to Halvor, as though seeking shelter against all the cruel gossip that was sure to follow now.
The men were speechless, mostly from astonishment at Karin Ingmarsson, who looked younger and more girlish than she ever had in her whole life.
Then Halvor said, his voice trembling with feeling, "Karin, when I got your father's watch, I felt nothing greater could ever happen to me. But what you've just done tops everything."
At that, Berger Sven Persson, who was in many ways a fine man, got to his feet.
"Let's all congratulate Karin and Halvor," he said graciously. "Everyone should know that the man Karin, daughter of Ingmar, has chosen is a man of true, sterling worth."

chapters.title: Book Two — In Zion
paragraphs: It’s not surprising that an old country schoolmaster should sometimes be a little too sure of himself: for nearly a lifetime he has been handing out knowledge and advice to his fellow men. He sees that all the local peasants live by what he’s taught them, and that not one of them knows more than what he, their schoolmaster, has told them. How could he help but think of everyone in the parish as mere schoolchildren, no matter how old they’ve grown? It’s only natural that he’d consider himself wiser than everybody else. It seems almost impossible for one of these old-fashioned schoolmasters to treat anyone as a full-grown adult, since he looks at each and every one of them as a child with dimpled cheeks and wide, innocent baby eyes.
One Sunday in winter, just after service, the pastor and the schoolmaster stood talking together in the vestry. The conversation had turned to the Salvation Army.
"It's a singular idea to have hit upon," the pastor remarked. "I never imagined I should live to see anything of that sort!"
The schoolmaster glanced sharply at the pastor. He thought the remark entirely irrelevant. Surely the pastor could never think that such an absurd innovation would find its way into their parish.
"I don't believe you are likely to see it, either," he said emphatically.
The pastor, knowing himself to be a weak and broken-down man, let the schoolmaster have things pretty much his own way. But all the same, he could not resist teasing him a little from time to time.

"How can you feel so certain that we shall escape the Salvation Army, Storm?" he said. "You see, when pastor and schoolmaster stand together, there's no danger of any nuisance of that sort crowding in."
To this the schoolmaster did not reply at once. Presently he said, quite meekly: "The pastor has never heard me preach."

The mission house was a genuine sore point. The clergyman had never once set foot in the place. And now that this touchy question had come up, both men regretted having said anything to hurt each other’s feelings. “Maybe I’m being unfair to Storm,” the pastor thought. “In the four years he’s been holding his Sunday afternoon Bible talks, attendance at the morning church service has actually gone up, and I haven’t seen the slightest sign of division in the church. Storm hasn’t destroyed the parish, the way I feared he would. He’s a faithful friend and servant, and I mean to show him how much I appreciate that.”
The little misunderstanding of the morning resulted in the pastor attending the schoolmaster's meeting that afternoon.
"I'll give Storm a pleasant surprise," he thought. "I will go to hear him preach in his Zion."

On the way to the mission house the pastor's thoughts went back to the time it was built. How full the air had been of prophecies, and how firmly he had believed that God had intended it to be something extraordinary—something far beyond what ordinary minds could conceive. But as one year after another had passed, and the only thing that happened was that the schoolmaster explained the Bible in his own solid but thoroughly orthodox way, the pastor had felt rather foolish for his enthusiasm.

The schoolmaster's Zion was a large hall with light-colored walls. On either side hung wood engravings of Luther and Melanchthon in fur-trimmed cloaks; along the borders, close to the ceiling, ran brightly illuminated Bible texts, decorated with flowers and heavenly trumpets and bassoons. At the front of the room, above the speaker's platform, hung an oleograph of the Good Shepherd.

The large bare room was full of people, which was all that seemed necessary to create an atmosphere of impressive solemnity. Most of the people were dressed in the picturesque peasant costume of the province, their cheeks ruddy with the cold winter air. The women sat with their prayerbooks in their hands, the men with their legs stretched out, their arms folded, and their eyes half shut.
Storm had already begun his address when he saw the pastor come down the aisle and take a seat in the front row.
"You're a wonderful man, Storm!" the schoolmaster thought. "Everything comes your way. Here's the pastor himself to do you honor."

During the time the schoolmaster had been holding meetings, he had explained the Bible from cover to cover. That afternoon he spoke of the Heavenly Jerusalem and everlasting bliss, as described in the book of Revelation. He spoke so beautifully of the New Jerusalem with its gates of pearl and its streets of gold that many of his listeners felt as if they could actually see it. Some of them went so far as to say that the air in the room suddenly became fresh and sweet, like the air in a garden of roses.

The pastor became interested when the schoolmaster began to talk about Jerusalem. The strange misgivings he had had long ago flashed through his mind again. In the middle of the service the little girl Gertrude's words came back to him: "I have destroyed the parish in order to build a Jerusalem."
Storm had no sooner said "Amen" than a voice from the group by the door piped up: "I should very much like to say a few words."
"That must be Hoek Matts Ericsson," thought the pastor, and others with him. For no one else in the parish had such a sweet and childlike treble.
The next moment a little meek-faced man made his way up to the platform, followed by a score of men and women who seemed to be there to support and encourage him.

The pastor, the schoolmaster, and the whole congregation sat there in suspense. “Hoek Matts must have come to tell us of some terrible calamity,” they thought. “Either the king is dead, or war has broken out, or maybe some poor soul has fallen into the river and drowned.” And yet Hoek Matts didn’t look like a man bringing bad news. He seemed earnest and a little stirred up, but at the same time he looked so pleased with himself that he could hardly keep from smiling.

“I want to say to the schoolmaster and to the congregation,” he began, “that a week ago last Sunday, while I was sitting at home with my family, the Spirit came down on me, and I started to preach. We couldn’t make it down here to hear Storm, on account of the ice and sleet, and we sat there longing to hear the Word of God. Then all at once I felt that I could speak myself. I’ve been preaching for two Sundays now, and my family at home, and our neighbors too, have all told me I ought to come down here and let everyone hear me.”
Hoek Matts also said he was astonished that the gift of speech should have fallen upon so humble a man. "But the schoolmaster himself is only a peasant," he added, with a little more confidence.
After this preamble, Hoek Matts folded his hands and was ready to begin preaching at once. But by that time the schoolmaster had recovered from his first shock of surprise.
"Do you think of speaking here now, Hoek Matts—immediately?"

"Yes, that's my intention," the man replied. He grew as frightened as a child when Storm glowered at him. "It was my purpose, of course, to first ask leave of the schoolmaster and the rest," he stammered.
"We're all through for the day," said Storm conclusively.

Then the meek little man began to beg, his voice near tears: "Won't you please let me say a few words? I only want to tell of the things that have come to me when walking behind the plow and when working in the forest. Just a few words—"

But the schoolmaster, though he had had such a day of triumph himself, felt no pity for the poor little man. "Matts Ericsson comes here with his own peculiar notions, and claims they are messages from the Holy Spirit. Can I allow any such thing? Should I open the door to one of these false prophets for a single moment? In my meeting I shall have the true faith, and no other!" he thought.
Hoek Matts dared not protest, and the schoolmaster opened the hymnbook.

"Let us all join in singing hymn one hundred and eighty-seven," he said. He read out the hymn in stentorian tones, then began to sing at the top of his voice: "Are your windows open toward Jerusalem?"
Meanwhile he thought: "It was well after all that the pastor happened in today. Now he can see that I know how to maintain order in my Zion."

But no sooner was the hymn finished than a man jumped to his feet. It was the proud and dignified Ljung Bjoern Olafsson, who was married to one of the Ingmar girls and owned a large farmstead near the Ingmar Farm.
"We down at this end think the schoolmaster might have consulted our wishes before turning Matts Ericsson down," he mildly protested.
"Oh, you think so, do you, sonny?" The schoolmaster spoke in just the kind of tone he would have used in reproving some young upstart. "Then let me tell you that no one but myself has any say here."

Ljung Bjoern turned blood red. He had not meant to provoke a quarrel with Storm, but had simply wished to soften the blow for Hoek Matts, who was an inoffensive man. All the same, he could not help feeling riled.
"Twice I have heard Hoek Matts preach, and must say he is wonderful. I believe everyone present would benefit from hearing him."

The schoolmaster answered pleasantly enough, but in the old admonishing tone of the classroom: "Surely you understand, Krister Larsson, that I can't allow this. If I were to let Hoek Matts preach today, then tomorrow some Waldenstromian or Baptist might come along and demand the same privilege. Ah, no, my dear Krister!"
At this several people laughed. But Ljung Bjoern was ready with a sharp reply: "I see no reason why Krister and I shouldn't be as well qualified to preach as the schoolmaster," he said.

Tims Halvor arose and tried to calm them and prevent possible strife. "Those of us who have furnished the money to build and run this mission should be consulted before any new preacher is brought in. So let us drop the matter for today and discuss it at the next business meeting."

By that time Krister Larsson had become worked up and was on his feet again. "I recall that when we built this hall, we all agreed it should be a free-for-all meeting house and not a church where only one man can preach. My opinion is that the schoolmaster has no more right to refuse Matts Ericsson than any of the rest of us."

When Krister had spoken, everyone seemed to breathe easier. Only an hour before, it had not occurred to them that they could ever wish to hear any speaker but the schoolmaster. Now they thought it would be rather nice to hear Hoek Matts, who was said to be inspired by God. Faces began to light up and voices grew excited.

There would likely have been no further disturbance if only Bullet Gunner had stayed away that day. He too was a brother-in-law of Tims Halvor—a tall, gaunt fellow with a shifty and cunning look. He was rather ill-thought-of in the parish, for he was never disposed to lend a helping hand. But he was sharp and ready with his tongue.
"There was a lot of talk about freedom while we were building this house," said Gunner, "but I haven't heard a liberal word since the place first opened."

The schoolmaster grew purple. Gunner's remark was the first sign of actual hostility. "Let me remind you, Bullet Gunner, that here you have heard the true freedom preached, as Luther himself preached it. And you ought to be grateful to the man who has stood here for years and given you words of truth!"

"The schoolmaster would have us think that everything new is worthless as soon as it touches on doctrine," Gunner replied, half soothingly, half mockingly. "He approves of our using new methods of farming and new machines, but he won't let us hear a word of any new kind of preaching."
Storm began to think that Bullet Gunner's bark was worse than his bite. "Is it your meaning," he said in a jesting tone, "that we should preach a different doctrine here from the Lutheran?"
"It is not a question of a new doctrine," roared Gunner, "but of who shall preach! And as far as I know, Matts Ericsson is as good a Lutheran as either the schoolmaster or the parson."

For the moment the schoolmaster had forgotten about the parson. But now he glanced down at him. The clergyman sat quietly musing, his chin resting on the knob of his cane. There was a curious gleam in his eye and a faint smile on his lips.

“Maybe it would have been just as well if the parson hadn’t come today after all,” the schoolmaster thought. What was happening now reminded Storm of something he’d seen before. It could get just like this in school sometimes, on a bright spring morning, when a little bird perched outside the schoolroom window and sang its heart out. Then all at once the children would beg and tease to be let out of their lessons; they’d abandon their studies and kick up such a fuss that it was almost impossible to bring them back to order. Something of the same sort had come over the congregation once Hoek Matts arrived. Still, the schoolmaster meant to show the pastor and everyone else that he was man enough to put down the mutiny. “First, I’ll leave them be and let the ringleaders talk themselves hoarse,” he thought, and went and sat down in a chair behind the table where the water bottle stood.

Instantly there arose against him a perfect storm of protests. By that time everyone had become swollen with the idea that they were all just as good as the schoolmaster. "Why should he be the only one to preach? Were there not enough gifted men in the parish? It would be refreshing to hear a different voice."

These ideas seemed new to most of them, yet from the talk it was clear they had been germinating in their minds ever since the schoolmaster built the mission house and showed them that a plain peasant could stand up and speak the Word of God.

After a while Storm said to himself: "This tantrum must have spent itself by now. Time to show them who is master here." He rose, pounded the table with his fist, and, in a voice that could be heard across half the parish, shouted: "If there is nothing more to say, you will all go home now!"
Some of them actually did get up, for they had all gone to Storm's school and knew that when their teacher rapped on the table, everybody had to obey. Yet the majority stubbornly kept their seats.
"The schoolmaster forgets that now we are grown men," said one. "But he still seems to think we should jump just because he happens to rap on the table!" said another.

They went right on talking about wanting to hear new speakers, and which ones they should bring in. They were already quarreling among themselves as to whether it should be the Waldenstromians or the Baptists. Some were set on the Mission Friends, and others on the Methodists. But all were agreed on one thing: they wanted somebody new.

The schoolmaster stood staring at the crowd as if he were looking at some weird monstrosity. For until that moment he had seen only the child in each face. But now all the round baby cheeks had become angular and weather-beaten. The sleepy child eyes had turned quick and crafty. And the foolish little mouths had acquired a firm, hard set. These were not children but men—hard-headed peasants who were not to be controlled through fear. It was as if a century had passed in a single hour.

The tumult continued, growing louder and louder. The schoolmaster kept still and let them rage. Bullet Gunner, Ljung Bjoern, and Krister Larsson led the attack. Hoek Matts, who was the innocent cause of all the commotion, kept trying to silence them, but no one would listen to him.
Once again the schoolmaster glanced down at the parson, who was still quietly musing, the same gleam in his eyes, which were fixed on the schoolmaster.

"He's probably thinking of that evening four years ago when I told him I would build a mission," thought Storm. "He was right, too. Everything has turned out just as he said it would: heresy, revolt, disorder! And just now this could not have come at a worse time." But through all this self-reproach the schoolmaster saw one thing clearly: the mission house had been at fault from the very beginning. It had drawn the people away from the old road and onto a new one.

The instant this became clear to the schoolmaster, his head went up and his back straightened. He drew from his pocket a small key of polished steel. It was the key to Zion! He held it out to the congregation.
"Now I'm going to lay this key upon the table," he said, "and I shall never touch it again, for I see now that it has unlocked the door to everything I had hoped to shut out."
The schoolmaster put the key down, took up his hat, and walked straight over to the pastor.
"I want to thank you, Parson, for coming to hear me today," he said, "for if you hadn't come today, you never could have heard me."

chapters.title: Book Two — The Wild Hunt
paragraphs: Plenty of people thought Elof Ersson deserved no peace in his grave, given how shamefully he had treated Karin and young Ingmar. He had deliberately made away with all his and Karin's money, so she would suffer hardship after his death. And he left the farm mortgaged so heavily that Karin would have had to hand it over to the creditors, if Halvor had not been rich enough to buy the property and pay off the debts. Ingmar Ingmarsson's twenty thousand kronor, of which Elof had been sole trustee, had vanished completely. Some people thought Elof had buried the money; others thought he had given it away. Either way, it was never found.

When Ingmar learned he was penniless, he asked Karin what he should do. He told his sister that more than anything he would like to become a teacher, and he asked her to let him stay on with the Storms until he was old enough for college. Down in the village, he said, he could always borrow books from the schoolmaster or the pastor, and besides, he could help Storm at the school by hearing the children read--good practice for him.
Karin turned this over in her mind before answering. "I suppose you wouldn't want to stay at home, now that you can't be master here?" she said.

When Storm's daughter heard that Ingmar was coming back to stay, she made a face. She thought that if they had to have a boy living with them, they might as well have the judge's good-looking son, Bertil, or cheerful Gabriel, son of Hoek Matts Ericsson.

Gertrude liked both Gabriel and Bertil, but she could not quite say what she felt about Ingmar. She liked him because he helped her with her lessons and obeyed her like a servant, but he could also make her thoroughly annoyed, since he was clumsy and dull and did not know how to play. She had to admire how hard he worked and how quickly he learned, yet at times she nearly despised him for never showing off what he could do.

Gertrude's head was always full of odd little fancies and dreams, which she confided to Ingmar. If he happened to be away for a few days, she grew restless and felt she had no one to talk to, but the moment he got back, she could hardly remember what she had been missing.

The girl had never thought of Ingmar as a boy with money and good family behind him; she treated him, if anything, as beneath her. But when she heard that Ingmar had become poor, she cried over it, and when he told her he would not try to win back his property but meant to earn his own living as a teacher, she was so indignant she could barely contain herself.
Heaven only knows everything she had once dreamed he would become!

The children at Storm's school were kept to a strict routine. They were held hard to their lessons, and only rarely allowed any fun. But all that changed the spring Storm gave up preaching. Then Mother Stina told him, "Now, Storm, we have to let the young ones be young. Remember, you and I were young too. Why, when we were seventeen we danced many a night from sundown to sunup."
So one Saturday night, when young Gabriel and Gunhild, the councilman's daughter, came to visit the Storms, they actually held a dance at the schoolhouse.

Gertrude was thrilled at being allowed to dance, but Ingmar would not join in. Instead he picked up a book and sat down on the sofa by the window. Gertrude tried again and again to get him to put the book down, but Ingmar, sulky and shy, would not budge. Mother Stina looked at him and shook her head. "You can tell he comes of old, old stock," she thought. "That kind can never really be young."
The three who danced had such a good time that they talked about going to a real dance the next Saturday evening, and asked the schoolmaster and Mother Stina what they thought of it.
"If you do your dancing at Strong Ingmar's, you have my blessing," said Mother Stina, "since you'll only meet respectable folk there."
Storm set a condition too. "I can't let Gertrude go to a dance unless Ingmar comes along to look after her," he said.
At that, all three rushed over to Ingmar and begged him to come along.
"No," he growled, without even looking up from his book.

"There's no use asking him," Gertrude said, in a tone that made Ingmar lift his eyes. She looked radiant after the dance, smiling scornfully, her eyes flashing as she turned away. It was plain how much she despised him for sitting there so ugly and sulky, like some cranky old man. Ingmar had to change his mind and say yes--there was no way around it.

A few evenings later, while Gertrude and Mother Stina sat spinning in the kitchen, the girl noticed her mother growing uneasy. Every so often Mother Stina stopped her wheel to listen. "I can't imagine what that noise is," she said. "Do you hear anything, Gertrude?"
"Yes, I do," the girl answered. "There must be someone upstairs in the classroom."
"Who could possibly be up there at this hour?" Mother Stina scoffed. "Just listen to that rustling and pattering, back and forth across the room!"
And sure enough, there was a rustling and pattering and thumping overhead that made both Gertrude and her mother feel uneasy.
"There must be someone up there," Gertrude insisted.
"There can't be," Mother Stina said. "I'll tell you something--this has been going on every night since you danced here."

Gertrude realized her mother had gotten it into her head that the house had been haunted ever since the dance. If that idea took root in Mother Stina's mind, there would be no more dancing for Gertrude.
"I'm going up to see what it is," said the girl, standing up, but her mother grabbed her skirt.
"I don't know if I dare let you go," she said.
"Nonsense, Mother. It's best we find out what it is."
"Then I'd better come with you," her mother decided.
They crept quietly up the stairs. At the door they were afraid to open it. Mother Stina bent down and peered through the keyhole. Then she gave a little chuckle.
"What's so funny, Mother?" asked Gertrude.
"See for yourself--just be quiet!"

Gertrude put her eye to the keyhole. Inside, the benches and desks had been pushed against the wall, and in the middle of the schoolroom, in a cloud of dust, Ingmar Ingmarsson was spinning around with a chair in his arms.
"Has Ingmar lost his mind?" Gertrude exclaimed.

"Shh!" her mother warned, pulling her away from the door and down the stairs. "He must be teaching himself to dance. I suppose he wants to know how, so he can dance at the party," she added with a smirk. Then Mother Stina began shaking with laughter. "He nearly scared the life out of me," she admitted. "Thank God he can be young for once!" When she had gotten over her laughing fit, she said, "You're not to breathe a word of this to anyone, do you hear!"

Saturday evening the four young people stood on the schoolhouse steps, ready to leave. Mother Stina looked them over with approval. The boys wore yellow buckskin breeches and green homespun waistcoats with bright red sleeves. Gunhild and Gertrude wore striped skirts trimmed with red cloth and white blouses with big puffed sleeves; flowered kerchiefs crossed over their bodices, and their aprons were just as flowered as the kerchiefs.

As the four of them walked along in the twilight of a perfect spring evening, no one said much for a long while. Now and then Gertrude glanced sideways at Ingmar, thinking of how he had practiced learning to dance. Whatever the reason--whether it was the memory of his strange dancing, or the anticipation of a real dance ahead--her thoughts turned light and airy. She managed to stay just a little behind the others so she could daydream undisturbed. She made up a little story in her head about how the trees had gotten their new leaves.

It happened like this, she thought: after sleeping peacefully all winter, the trees suddenly began to dream. They dreamed that summer had come. They seemed to see the fields dressed in green grass and swaying grain; the hawthorn shimmering with fresh-blown roses; brooks and ponds spread with water-lily leaves; the stones hidden under the creeping vines of the twinflower, and the forest floor thick with starflowers. And amid all this finery, the trees saw themselves standing bare and gaunt. They grew ashamed of their nakedness, the way one does in dreams.
In their confusion and shame, the trees imagined everyone was laughing at them. The bumblebees came buzzing up to mock them, the magpies jeered, and the other birds sang taunting songs.
"Where will we find something to wear?" the trees asked in despair. But they had not a single leaf on any twig or branch, and their distress was so terrible that it woke them up.
Looking around, still half asleep, their first thought was: "Thank God, it was only a dream! There's certainly no summer around here yet. Lucky for us we haven't overslept."

But looking more closely, they noticed the streams were free of ice, blades of grass and crocuses were poking up from the soil, and under their own bark the sap was running. "Well, spring is here at least," said the trees, "so it's good we woke up. We've slept long enough this year--high time we got dressed."

So the birches quickly put on some sticky pale-green leaves, and the maples a few green flowers. The alder's leaves came out so crinkled and unfinished-looking that they seemed almost deformed, but the slender willow leaves slipped smooth and shapely from their buds right from the start.
Gertrude smiled to herself as she walked along, making all this up. She only wished she had been alone with Ingmar so she could have told it to him.

They had a long way to go to reach the Ingmar Farm--more than an hour's walk. They followed the riverside, and the whole time Gertrude stayed a little behind the others. Her imagination had begun playing with the red glow of the sunset, which now flared over the river, now over the bank. Gray alder and green birch were wrapped in the shimmer, flashing red one moment and taking on their true colors the next.
Suddenly Ingmar stopped, breaking off in the middle of something he was saying.
"What's wrong, Ingmar?" asked Gunhild.

Ingmar, pale as a ghost, stood staring at something ahead. The others saw only a wide plain covered with grainfields and ringed by hills, and in the middle of it a large farmstead. At that moment the sunset glow lay over the farm; every windowpane glittered, and the old roofs and walls had a bright red gleam about them.
Gertrude quickly went over to the others, and after a glance at Ingmar, drew Gunhild and Gabriel aside.

"We mustn't ask him anything about this place," she said under her breath. "That's the Ingmar Farm over there. The sight of it has probably made him sad. He hasn't been home in two years--not since he lost all his money."
The road they had taken led past the farm and down to Strong Ingmar's cabin, at the edge of the forest.

Soon Ingmar came running back, calling, "Hadn't we better go this way instead?" Then he led them onto a bypath that curved around the edge of the forest, by which they could reach the cabin without crossing the farm itself.
"You know Strong Ingmar, I take it?" said Gabriel.
"Oh, yes," young Ingmar answered. "We used to be good friends, back in the old days."
"Is it true he knows magic?" asked Gunhild.
"Well--no," Ingmar answered, hesitating, as if half believing it himself.
"You might as well tell us what you know," Gunhild pressed.
"The schoolmaster says we mustn't believe in things like that."
"The schoolmaster can't stop a person from seeing what he sees and believing what he knows," Gabriel declared.

Ingmar wanted to tell them all about his home; memories of his childhood came flooding back at the sight of the old place. "I can tell you about something I saw once," he said. "It happened one winter when Father and Strong Ingmar were up in the forest, tending the charcoal kiln. When Christmas came around, Strong Ingmar offered to watch the kiln alone so Father could come home for the holidays. The day before Christmas, Mother sent me up to the forest with a basket of good food for Strong Ingmar. I started early, so I'd get there before the midday meal. When I arrived, Father and Strong Ingmar had just finished drawing a kiln, and all the charcoal had been spread out on the ground to cool. It was still smoking, and where the coals lay thickest it was close to catching fire, which must never be allowed to happen. Preventing that is the most important part of the whole business of making charcoal. So Father said, the moment he saw me: 'I'm afraid you'll have to go home alone, little Ingmar. I can't leave Strong Ingmar with all this work.' Strong Ingmar walked along the side of the pile where the smoke rose thickest. 'You go on, Big Ingmar,' he said. 'I've handled worse than this.' After a while the smoke died down some. 'Now let's see what kind of Christmas treat Brita's sent me,' said Strong Ingmar, taking the basket from me. 'Come, let me show you what a fine house we've got here.' Then he took me into the hut where he and Father lived. At the back was a rough stone, and the other walls were made of spruce and blackthorn branches. 'Well, lad, I bet you never guessed your father had a royal castle like this out in the forest, eh?' said Strong Ingmar. 'Here are walls that keep out both storm and frost,' he laughed, poking his arm straight through the spruce branches.

"Soon Father came in laughing. He and the old man were black with soot and smelled of sour charcoal smoke. But I'd never seen Father so happy and full of fun. Neither of them could stand up straight in the hut, and the only furniture in the place was two bunks made of spruce twigs and a couple of flat stones they'd built a fire on--yet they were perfectly content. They sat down side by side on one of the bunks and opened the basket. 'I don't know if you can have any of this,' Strong Ingmar said to Father, 'seeing as it's my Christmas dinner, you know.' 'Since it's Christmas Eve, you'll have to be good to me,' said Father. 'At a time like this, I suppose it wouldn't do to let a poor old charcoal burner starve,' Strong Ingmar said then.

"They went on like that the whole time they were eating. Mother had sent along a little brandy with the food. I marveled that people could be so happy over food and drink. 'You'll have to tell your mother that Big Ingmar's eaten up everything,' the old man said, 'and that she'll have to send more tomorrow.' 'So I see,' I said.
