"Just then I was startled by a crackling noise from the fireplace. It sounded like someone had thrown a handful of pebbles onto the stones. Father didn't notice, but Strong Ingmar said at once, 'What, already?' Still, he kept eating. Then there was more crackling, louder this time--it sounded like a shovelful of stones thrown on the fire. 'Well, well, is it that urgent?' Strong Ingmar exclaimed, and went outside. 'The charcoal must be on fire!' he called back. 'Just sit still, Big Ingmar. I'll see to it myself.' Father and I sat very quiet.

"After a while Strong Ingmar came back, and the fun started up again. 'I haven't had such a merry Christmas in years,' he laughed. He had barely gotten the words out when the crackling started again. 'What, again? Well, I never!' and out he flew in an instant. The charcoal had caught fire again. When the old man came back the second time, Father said to him, 'I see now you've got such good help up here you can manage on your own.' 'Yes, you can safely go home and keep your Christmas, Big Ingmar--there are those here who'll help me.' Then Father and I went home, and everything turned out fine. And never, before or after, did any kiln Strong Ingmar tended ever catch fire."

Gunhild thanked Ingmar for the story, but Gertrude walked on in silence, as though she had gotten frightened. It was starting to get dark; everything that had looked so rosy a little while before was now blue or gray. Here and there in the forest a shiny leaf gleamed in the twilight like the red eye of a troll.

Gertrude was surprised that Ingmar had talked so much, and for so long. He seemed like a different person since coming onto his home ground--he held his head higher than usual and walked with a firmer step. Gertrude did not much like this change in him; it made her uneasy. All the same she rallied, and started teasing Ingmar about going home to dance.

Then at last they came to a little gray hut. Candles burned inside--the windows were too small to let in much light. They caught the sound of fiddle music and the stamp of dancing feet. Still the girls paused, puzzled. "Is this it?" they asked. "Can anyone dance in there? The place looks too small to hold even one couple."
"Go on inside," said Gabriel. "The hut isn't as small as it looks."

Outside the open door stood a group of boys and girls who had danced themselves into a warm glow; the girls were fanning themselves with their head-shawls, and the boys had pulled off their short black jackets to dance in their bright green, red-sleeved waistcoats.
The newcomers pushed their way through the crowd at the door and into the hut. The first person they saw was Strong Ingmar--a small, stout man with a big head and a long beard.
"He must be kin to the elves and the trolls," Gertrude thought. The old man stood on the hearth, playing his fiddle, so as not to get in the dancers' way.

The hut was larger than it had looked from outside, but poor and rundown. The bare pine walls were worm-eaten, the beams blackened with smoke. There were no curtains at the windows and no cloth on the table. It was clear Strong Ingmar lived alone. All his children had left him for America, and the old man's only pleasure in his loneliness was gathering the young people around him on Saturday nights and letting them dance to his fiddle.

It was dim in the hut, and stiflingly close. Couple after couple whirled around inside. Gertrude could hardly breathe and wanted to hurry back out, but it was impossible to get past the tight wall of people blocking the doorway.

Strong Ingmar played with a steady hand and perfect timing, but the instant young Ingmarsson stepped into the room, he dragged his bow across the strings in a rasping screech that stopped all the dancers cold. "It's nothing!" he shouted. "Go on with the dance!"

Ingmar put his arm around Gertrude's waist to join the dance. Gertrude looked quite surprised that he wanted to dance at all. But they could not get anywhere, since the dancers followed one another so closely that no one who had not been there from the start could squeeze in between them.
The old man stopped short, rapped his bow against the fender, and said in a commanding voice: "Make room for Big Ingmar's son whenever there's dancing in my shack!"
At that, everyone turned to look at Ingmar, who grew so embarrassed he could not move. Gertrude had to grab hold of him and practically drag him across the floor.

As soon as the dance ended, the fiddler came down to greet Ingmar. Feeling Ingmar's hand in his, the old man pretended great alarm and instantly let go of it. "Goodness!" he exclaimed. "Careful with those delicate schoolmaster hands! A clumsy old fellow like me could easily crush them."

He led young Ingmar and his friends up to the table, shooing away several old women who had been sitting there watching. Then he went over to the cupboard and brought out bread and butter and root beer.
"I don't usually serve refreshments at these gatherings," he said. "Everyone else has to be content with music and dancing, but Ingmar Ingmarsson has to have a bite to eat under my roof."
Pulling up a little three-legged stool, the old man sat down in front of Ingmar and studied him sharply.
"So, going to be a schoolteacher, are you?" he asked.
Ingmar closed his eyes for a moment, the shadow of a smile on his lips, but he answered rather gloomily all the same: "They've got no use for me at home."
"No use for you?" the old man cried. "You've no idea how soon they might need you on the farm. Elof only lasted two years--who knows how long Halvor will hold out?"
"Halvor's a strong, healthy man," Ingmar pointed out.
"Surely you know Halvor will hand the farm over to you the moment you're able to buy it back."
"He'd be a fool to give up the Ingmar Farm now that it's fallen into his hands."

All through this exchange Ingmar sat gripping the edge of the plain deal table. Suddenly there was a cracking sound. Ingmar had broken a corner off the table. "If you become a schoolteacher, he'll never let you have the farm," the old man went on.
"You think so?"
"Think? What's there to think--it's plain enough how you've been raised. Have you ever driven a plow?"
"No."
"Or tended a kiln, or felled a big pine?"
Ingmar sat there looking perfectly calm, but the table kept crumbling under his fingers. Finally the old man noticed.

"See here, young man!" he said, when he saw what was happening. "I'll have to take you in hand again." Then he picked up some of the table's splinters and tried to fit them back into place. "You rascal! You ought to be touring the fairs, showing off tricks like that for money!" he laughed, giving Ingmar a hard slap on the shoulder. "Oh, you'd make a fine schoolteacher, you would!"

In a flash he was back at the fireplace, fiddling away. Now there was snap and drive in his playing. He beat time with his foot and set the dancers spinning. "This is young Ingmar's polka!" he called out. "Hoop-la! Now the whole house has to dance for young Ingmar!"

Two such pretty girls as Gertrude and Gunhild naturally had to be in every dance. Ingmar did not dance much. He spent most of the time talking with some of the older men at the far end of the room. Between dances, people crowded around him as if it did them good just to look at him.

Gertrude thought Ingmar had forgotten her entirely, which made her quite miserable. "Now he feels he's Big Ingmar's son, and I'm just the schoolmaster's Gertrude," she sulked. It struck her as strange that she should take this so much to heart. Between dances, some of the young people stepped outside for air. The night had turned bitterly cold. It was quite dark, and since no one wanted to head home yet, they all said, "Let's wait a little; the moon will be up soon. It's too dark to start home now."

Once, when Ingmar and Gertrude happened to be standing outside the door, the old man came and pulled the boy away. "Come, let me show you something," he said, and taking Ingmar's hand, led him through a thicket a short way from the house. "Now stand still and look down," he said. Ingmar found himself looking down into a cleft, at the bottom of which something white glimmered. "This must be Langfors Rapids," young Ingmar said.
"Right you are," the old man nodded. "Now, what do you suppose a waterfall like that could be used for, eh?"
"It could run a mill," Ingmar said thoughtfully.

The old man chuckled to himself. He patted Ingmar on the back, then gave him a poke in the ribs that nearly sent him into the rapids. "But who's going to put up a mill here? Who's going to get rich off it, and who's going to buy back the Ingmar Farm, eh?" he chuckled.
"I'd like to know myself," said Ingmar.

Then the old man began laying out a big plan he had been turning over: Ingmar was to persuade Tims Halvor to build a sawmill below the rapids, and afterward lease it to him. For years the old man had dreamed of finding some way for Big Ingmar's son to come into his own again. Ingmar stood quietly gazing down at the foaming rapids.

"Come, let's get back to the house and the dancing," said the old man, but since Ingmar did not move, he waited patiently. "If he's the right sort, he won't answer this today, or tomorrow either," he thought to himself. "An Ingmarsson needs time to think things over."
And as they stood there, they suddenly heard a sharp, angry bark, as if from some dog running loose in the forest.
"Do you hear that, Ingmar?" the old man asked.
"Yes--that must be a dog on the rampage."

Then they heard the bark more clearly; it seemed to be coming closer, as though the animal were heading straight for the hut. The old man grabbed Ingmar by the wrist. "Come, boy!" he said. "Get inside, quick as you can!"
"What's wrong?" asked Ingmar, startled.
"Get inside, I tell you!"
As they hurried toward the hut, the angry barking sounded as if it were right on top of them.
"What kind of dog is that?" Ingmar kept asking.

"Get inside, just get inside!" the old man cried, shoving Ingmar into the narrow passage. Before shutting the outer door, he shouted, "If any of you are still out there, come in now!" Holding the door open, he watched people come running from every direction. "In with you, in with you!" he shrieked, stamping his feet impatiently.
Meanwhile the people inside the hut were growing frightened. They all wanted to know what was wrong. Once the old man was sure everyone was in, he shut and bolted the door.

"Are you out of your minds, running around when you hear the mountain dog!" Just then the barking sounded right outside the hut; it was as if the mountain dog were circling the house again and again, letting out hideous howls.
"Isn't it just a regular dog?" a young farmhand asked.
"Go on out and call to it yourself, if you like, Nils Jansson."

Then everyone fell silent, listening to the howling thing circle the house without a break. It sounded eerie and dreadful. They began to shudder and shake, and some turned white as death. No, this was clearly no ordinary dog--anyone could tell that. It had to be some demon loosed from hell, they thought.
The little old man was the only one still moving. First he closed the flue, then went around snuffing out the candles.
"No, no!" the women cried. "Don't put out the lights!"
"You must let me do what's best for all of us," the old man said.
One of the girls grabbed his coat. "Is the mountain dog dangerous?" she asked.
"No, not him--but what comes after."
"And what comes after?"
The old man listened again. Then he said, "Now we must all be very still."

At once there was breathless silence. Once more the terrible howling seemed to circle the hut, but it grew fainter as it moved off across the marsh and up the mountains on the far side of the valley. Then came an ominous stillness. Presently one man, unable to hold his tongue any longer, said the dog had gone.
Without a word, Strong Ingmar raised his hand and struck the man across the mouth.

From far off, at the top of Mount Flack, came a piercing sound; it was like a howling wind, but it could also have been a blast from a horn. Now and again a long blare rang out, then a roaring and tramping and snorting.

All at once the thing came rushing down from the mountain with a terrible roar. They could tell when it reached the foot of the slope, when it swept along the edge of the forest, and when it was directly overhead. It was like thunder rolling across the earth--as if the whole mountain had come crashing down into the valley. When it seemed almost upon them, every head bowed. "It will crush us," they all thought. "It will surely crush us."

But what they felt was not so much fear of death as terror that this might be the prince of darkness himself, come with all his demons. What frightened them most were the shrieks and moans rising above the other noise. There were wails and groans, laughter and bellowing, whining and hissing. When what they had taken for a huge thunderstorm was right on top of them, it seemed to be a mixture of groans and curses, sobs and angry cries, blaring horns, crackling fire, the wailing of doomed spirits, the mocking laughter of demons, and the beating of huge wings.

They believed all the furies of hell had been let loose that night and would sweep them away. The ground shook, and the hut swayed as though it would topple over. It was as if wild horses were rearing on the roof, as if howling ghosts were rushing past the door, and as if owls and bats were beating their wings against the chimney.
While this was happening, someone put an arm around Gertrude's waist and drew her down to her knees. Then she heard Ingmar whisper: "We must kneel, Gertrude, and ask God to help us."
Only a moment before, Gertrude had thought she was dying, the fear gripping her was so terrible. "I don't mind dying," she thought. "What's awful is that the powers of evil are hovering over us."

But no sooner had Gertrude felt Ingmar's arm protecting her than her heart began to beat again, and the numbness left her limbs. She pressed close to him. She was not afraid anymore. How strange--Ingmar must have been frightened too, and yet he could still give her a feeling of safety and protection.

At last the terrible noises died away; only the faintest echoes reached them from a distance. They seemed to follow the trail of the dog, down through the marsh and up into the mountain passes beyond Olaf's Peak.

And yet the silence in Strong Ingmar's hut remained unbroken. No one moved, no one spoke; at times it was as though fear had snuffed out all life in the room. Now and then a deep sigh broke the stillness. No one moved for a long, long time. Some stood pressed against the walls, others had sunk onto the benches, but most knelt on the floor in anxious prayer. Everyone was motionless, stunned with fear.

Hour after hour passed like this, and during that time more than one person in the room searched their soul and resolved to live differently from now on--closer to God, further from His enemies--for each of them thought: "It's something I did that brought this on us. This happened because of my sins. I could hear the fiends calling to me and threatening me, shrieking my name as they rushed by."
As for Gertrude, her only thought was: "I know now I can never live without Ingmar. I have to stay near him, because of the way he makes me feel safe."

Then gradually the day began to break; the faint light of dawn crept into the hut, showing the many pale faces. A bird twittered, then another, and another. Strong Ingmar's cow began lowing for her breakfast, and his cat, who never slept indoors on nights there was dancing, came to the door and meowed. But no one inside moved until the sun rose over the eastern hills. Then, one by one, they slipped out without a word or even a goodbye.

Outside, the departing guests saw the signs of the night's devastation. A huge pine that had stood close to the gate had been torn up by the roots and thrown down; branches and fence posts lay scattered over the ground; bats and owls had been crushed against the walls of the hut.
Along the broad road leading up Mount Klack, every tree had been blown down. No one could bear to look at it for long, so they all hurried on toward the village.

It was Sunday, and most people were still in bed, though a few were already out tending their cattle. An old man had just come out of his house with his Sunday coat, to brush and air it. From another house came a father, mother, and children, all dressed for a holiday outing. It was a great relief to see people going quietly about their business, unaware of the terrible things that had happened in the forest during the night.

At last they reached the riverside, where the houses stood closer together, and then the village itself. They were glad to see the old church and everything else. It was comforting to find everything down here looking ordinary: the shop sign creaked on its hinges as always, the post-office horn hung in its usual place, and the innkeeper's dog lay sleeping outside his kennel, same as ever. It was also a happy surprise to see a little bird-cherry bush that had bloomed overnight, and the green benches in the pastor's garden, which must have been set out late the evening before. All of this was deeply reassuring. But still, no one dared speak until they had each reached their own home.
When Gertrude stood on the schoolhouse steps, she said to Ingmar: "I've danced my last dance, Ingmar."
"So have I," Ingmar said solemnly.
"And you'll become a minister, won't you, Ingmar? And if you can't be a preacher, at least be a teacher. There's so much evil in the world to fight against."
Ingmar looked straight at Gertrude. "What did those voices say to you?" he asked.
"They said I'd gotten caught up in the snares of sin, and that the devil would come and take me, because I loved dancing so much."

"Now let me tell you what I heard," said Ingmar. "It seemed to me that all the old Ingmarssons were cursing and threatening me, because I wanted to be something more than a peasant, and do something besides just working the soil and the forest."

chapters.title: Book Two — Hellgum
paragraphs: The night of the dance at Strong Ingmar's, Tims Halvor was away, and his wife Karin slept alone in the little room off the living room. During the night Karin had a terrifying dream. She dreamed that Elof was alive and throwing a wild party. She could hear him in the next room clinking glasses, laughing loudly, singing filthy songs. In the dream, Elof and his cronies grew noisier and noisier, until it sounded as if they were smashing the tables and chairs. Karin grew so frightened that she woke up. But even after waking, the noise went on. The earth shook, the windows rattled, roof tiles worked loose, and the old pear trees by the gables lashed the house with their thick branches. It was as if Judgment Day had come.

Just as the noise reached its height, a windowpane burst, and the shattered glass fell jingling to the floor. A violent gust of wind swept through the room, and then Karin thought she heard a laugh right at her ear--the same laugh she had heard in the dream. She thought she was about to die. She had never felt such terror; her heart stopped, and her whole body went numb and cold as ice.

All at once the noise died away, and Karin, as it were, came back to life. The raw night wind swept into the room, so after a moment Karin decided to get up and stuff something into the broken pane. But as she stepped out of bed, her legs gave way, and she found she could not walk. She did not cry out for help, but lay back down quietly. "I'll surely be able to walk once I've calmed down," she thought. After a few moments she tried again. This time too her legs failed her, and she fell flat on the floor beside the bed.

In the morning, once people were up and about in the house, the doctor was sent for. He could not figure out what had come over Karin. She did not seem ill, and she was not paralyzed. He decided her trouble must have been brought on by fright.

"You'll soon be all right again," he assured her. Karin listened to the doctor but said nothing. She was certain Elof had been in the room that night, and that he was the cause of her condition. She also had a feeling she would never recover from this shock.

All that morning she sat up in bed and brooded. She tried to work out why God had let this trial come upon her. She examined her conscience thoroughly, but could not find any particular sin that deserved such a terrible punishment. "God is being unjust to me," she thought.
That afternoon she was taken to Storm's mission house, where at the time a lay preacher named Dagson was leading the meetings. She hoped he could tell her why she had been punished this way.

Dagson was a popular speaker, and he had never had so many listeners as that afternoon. My, what a crowd there was down at the mission house! No one talked of anything but what had happened that night at Strong Ingmar's hut. The whole parish was terrified, and had turned out in full force to hear the Word of God preached with a force strong enough to shatter their fears. Hardly a quarter of them could fit inside, but the windows and doors stood wide open, and Dagson had such a powerful voice he could be heard even by those outside. Of course he knew what had happened and what people wanted to hear. He opened his sermon with a terrifying picture of hell and the prince of darkness. He reminded them of the evil one who lurks in the dark to capture souls, who lays the snares of sin and sets the traps of vice. The people shuddered. They seemed to see a world full of devils, tempting and luring them to ruin. Everything was sin, everything was danger. They were wandering among pitfalls, hunted and tormented like wild beasts of the forest. When Dagson spoke like this, his voice cut through the room like a blasting wind, and his words were like tongues of fire.

Everyone who heard Dagson's sermon compared it to a roaring torrent of flame. With all his talk of demons and fire and smoke, they felt just as they would if trapped in a burning forest--when fire creeps along the moss beneath your feet, smoke fills the air you breathe, the heat singes your hair, the roar of flames fills your ears, and flying sparks catch your clothes on fire.

That was how Dagson drove the people through flame and smoke and ruin. They had fire in front of them, fire behind them, fire to the left and right, and saw nothing ahead but destruction. Yet after leading them through all these horrors, he finally brought them to a green spot in the forest, peaceful and cool and safe. In the middle of a flowering meadow sat Jesus, arms outstretched to the fleeing, hunted men and women who threw themselves at His feet. Now all danger was past, and they suffered no more distress or persecution.
Dagson spoke exactly as he himself felt. If he could only lay himself down at Jesus' feet, a great peace and calm would come over him, and he would have no more fear of the world's snares.

After the service there was a great outpouring of emotion. Many people rushed up to the preacher to thank him, tears streaming down their faces. They told him his words had awakened in them a true faith in God. But through all this Karin sat unmoved. When Dagson finished speaking, she lifted her heavy eyelids and looked at him, as though reproaching him for giving her nothing. Just then someone outside cried out, loud enough for the whole congregation to hear:
"Woe, woe, woe to those who give stones for bread! Woe, woe, woe to those who give stones for bread!"

At that, everyone rushed outside, curious to see who had spoken those words, leaving Karin sitting there helplessly. Presently members of her own household came back and told her the person who had cried out was a tall, dark stranger. He and a pretty, fair-haired woman had been seen coming down the road in a cart during the service. They had stopped to listen, and just as they were about to drive on, the man had stood up and spoken. Some people thought they recognized the woman--they said she was one of Strong Ingmar's daughters, one of those who had gone to America and married there. The man was evidently her husband. Of course it is not easy to recognize someone you knew as a girl in ordinary peasant dress, once she comes back a grown woman dressed in city clothes.

Karin and the stranger clearly felt the same way about Dagson. Karin never went back to the mission house. But later that summer, when a Baptist layman came through the parish baptizing and preaching, she went to hear him, and when the Salvation Army began holding meetings in the village, she attended one of those too.

The parish was caught up in a great religious upheaval. At every meeting there were awakenings and conversions. People seemed to find what they had been looking for. Yet among all the preachers Karin had heard, not one could give her any comfort.

A blacksmith named Birger Larsson had a smithy close to the highroad. His shop was small and dark, with a low door and just a hole for a window. Birger Larsson made plain knives, mended locks, and fitted tires to wheels and sled runners. When there was nothing else to do, he forged nails.

One summer evening there was a rush of work at the smithy. At one anvil stood Birger Larsson, flattening nailheads; his eldest son worked another anvil, forging iron rods and cutting off pins. A second son worked the bellows, a third carried coal to the forge, turned the iron, and brought it to the smiths when it was white-hot. The fourth son, no more than seven, gathered up the finished nails, tossed them into a trough of water, then bunched and tied them.

While they were all hard at work, a stranger came up and stood in the doorway. He was a tall, swarthy-looking man, and had to bend nearly double to look in. Birger Larsson glanced up from his work to see what he wanted.

"I hope you don't mind my looking in, though I've got no particular business here," said the stranger. "I was a blacksmith myself in my younger days, and I can never pass a smithy without stopping to watch the work."

Birger Larsson noticed the man had large, sinewy hands--proper blacksmith's hands. He began asking at once who the man was and where he had come from. The man answered pleasantly, without giving his name. Birger found him clever and likable, and after showing him around the shop, went outside with him and started bragging about his sons. He had had hard times, he said, before the boys were big enough to help with the work, but now that they could all lend a hand, everything was going well. "In a few years I expect to be a rich man," he declared.

The stranger smiled a little and said he was glad to hear Birger's sons were such a help to him. Then, laying his heavy hand on Birger's shoulder and looking him straight in the eye, he said: "Since your sons have helped you so well in worldly matters, I suppose you let them help you in spiritual matters too?" Birger stared, dumbfounded. "I see this is a new idea to you," the stranger added. "Think it over till we meet again." Then he walked off smiling, and Birger Larsson, scratching his head, went back to his work. But the stranger's question haunted him for several days afterward. "I wonder what made him say that," he mused. "There must be something behind it I don't understand."

The day after the stranger spoke with Birger Larsson, something extraordinary happened at Tims Halvor's old shop, which since his marriage to Karin had passed to his brother-in-law, Bullet Gunner. Gunner was away at the time, and in his absence Brita Ingmarsson minded the shop. Brita was named for her mother, Big Ingmar's beautiful wife, whose looks she had inherited. In fact she had the reputation of being the prettiest girl ever born and raised on the Ingmar Farm. Though she bore no outward resemblance to the old Ingmars, she was every bit as upright and conscientious as any of them.

When Gunner was away, Brita always ran things her own way. Whenever old Corporal Felt came stumbling in, tipsy and shaky, wanting a bottle of beer, Brita gave him a flat "No," and when poor Kolbjörn's Lena came in wanting to buy a fancy brooch, Brita sent her home with several pounds of rye meal instead. A peasant woman who came in for some flimsy, showy fabric was told to go home and weave herself something sturdy and useful on her own loom. And no children dared come into the shop to spend their few coppers on candy and raisins while Brita was in charge.

That day Brita had few customers. For hour after hour she sat alone, staring into space, despair burning in her eyes. Eventually she got up and took out a rope, then carried a small stepladder from the shop into the back room. She made a loop in one end of the rope and fastened the other end to a hook in the ceiling. Just as she was about to slip her head into the noose, she happened to glance down.

At that moment the door opened and a tall, dark man walked in. He had evidently entered the shop without her hearing him, and finding no one at the counter, had stepped behind it and opened the door to the back room.

Brita quietly climbed down from the ladder. The man did not speak, but withdrew into the shop, with Brita slowly following. She had never seen him before. She noticed his black curly hair, his throat-whiskers, his sharp eyes, and his big, sinewy hands. He was well dressed, but carried himself like a laborer. After sitting down on a rickety chair by the door, he began staring hard at Brita.

By then Brita was standing behind the counter again. She did not ask what he wanted; she only wished he would leave. The man simply stared and stared, never taking his eyes off her. Brita felt held by his gaze, unable to move. Presently she grew impatient and said, in her mind: "What's the use of you sitting there watching me? Don't you understand I'm going to do what I want to do anyway, the moment I'm left alone? If this were something that could be fixed," Brita argued silently, "I wouldn't mind you stopping me, but it can't be helped now."
All the while the man sat gazing intently at her.

"Let me tell you, we Ingmars aren't cut out to be shopkeepers," Brita went on in her thoughts. "You have no idea how happy Gunner and I were before he took up this business. People certainly warned me against marrying him--they didn't like his black hair, his sharp eyes, his quick tongue. But we were fond of each other, you see, and there was never a cross word between us until Gunner took over the shop. Since then things haven't been right. I want him to run the business my way. I can't stand him selling wine and beer to drunkards, and it seems to me he ought to encourage people to buy only what's useful and necessary, but Gunner thinks that's a ridiculous idea. Neither of us will budge, so we're forever quarreling, and now he doesn't care for me anymore."
She shot the man a fierce look, amazed that he would not give in to her silent pleading.

"Surely you can see I can't go on living with the shame of knowing he lets the bailiff seize poor people's belongings--takes their only cow, or a couple of sheep! Can't you see this will never come right? Why don't you go, and let me put an end to it all?"
Under the man's gaze, Brita gradually grew calmer, and after a while she began to cry softly. She was touched that he sat there, protecting her against herself.

As soon as the man saw Brita crying, he rose and went toward the door. On the doorstep he turned and looked straight into her eyes again, and said in a deep voice: "Do not harm yourself, for the time is coming when you shall live in righteousness."

Then he went on his way. She could hear his heavy footsteps as he walked off down the road. Brita ran into the little room, took down the rope, and carried the stepladder back into the shop. Then she sat down on a box and stayed there quietly for two full hours, lost in thought. She felt, somehow, that she had been wandering for a long time in a darkness so thick she could not see her hand in front of her face. She had lost her way and did not know where she had strayed, and with every step she had feared sinking into a bog or stumbling headlong into a pit. Now someone had called out to her to go no farther, but to sit down and wait for daybreak. She was glad she would not have to keep up her dangerous wandering; now she sat quietly, waiting for the dawn.

Strong Ingmar had a daughter named Anna Lisa. She had lived in Chicago for a number of years, and had married a Swede there named John Hellgum, the leader of a small band of believers with their own faith and doctrine. The day after the memorable dance night at Strong Ingmar's, Anna Lisa and her husband came home to visit her old father.

Hellgum spent his time taking long walks around the parish. He struck up conversations with everyone he met along the way. At first he would talk about ordinary things, but just before parting with someone, he would always lay his big hand on their shoulder and say a few words of comfort or warning.

Strong Ingmar saw very little of his son-in-law that summer, since he and young Ingmar, who had moved back to the Ingmar Farm by then, were working hard by day putting up a sawmill below the rapids. It was a proud day for Strong Ingmar when the sawmill was finished and the buzzing saws turned the first log into white planks.

One evening, walking home from work, the old man met Anna Lisa on the road. She looked frightened and seemed about to run off. Seeing this, Strong Ingmar quickened his pace, thinking something must be wrong at home. When he reached his hut he stopped short, frowning. As far back as he could remember, a certain rosebush had grown outside the door. It had been the apple of his eye--he had never let anyone pick a rose or even a leaf from it. Strong Ingmar had always tended the bush carefully, believing it sheltered elves and fairies. But now it had been cut down. Of course it must have been his son-in-law, the preacher, who had done it--the sight of the bush had always been an eyesore to him.

Strong Ingmar had his axe with him, and his grip on the handle tightened as he stepped into the hut. Inside sat Hellgum with an open Bible before him. He looked up and gave the old man a piercing stare, then went back to his reading--aloud, this time:

"Even as you think, we will be as the heathen, as the families of other lands, serving wood and stone--it shall not be at all as you think. As I live, says the Lord God, with a mighty hand, with an outstretched arm, and with fury poured out, I will rule over you--"

Without a word Strong Ingmar turned and walked out of the house. That night he slept in the barn. The next day he and Ingmar Ingmarsson set off for the forest to burn charcoal and fell timber. They were to be gone the whole winter.

On two or three occasions Hellgum had spoken at prayer meetings and laid out his teaching, which he insisted was the only true Christianity. But Hellgum was not as eloquent a speaker as Dagson, and he had won no converts. People who had met him informally and heard him say only a few striking words expected great things of him, but when he tried to give a long sermon, he turned heavy, dull, and tiresome.

Toward the end of summer Karin sank into utter despair over her condition. She rarely spoke. All day she sat motionless in her chair. She stopped going to hear preachers and stayed home, brooding over her misfortune. Now and then she would repeat to Halvor her father's old saying, that the Ingmars had nothing to fear so long as they walked in the ways of God. Now she had come to believe there was no truth in it, even that.
Halvor, not knowing what else to do, once suggested she talk to the newest preacher, but Karin said she would never again look to a parson for help.

One Sunday, toward the end of August, Karin sat at the window in the living room. A Sabbath stillness lay over the farm, and she could barely keep her eyes open. Her head kept sinking lower and lower toward her chest, until at last she dozed off.
She was suddenly woken by a voice just outside her window. She could not see who was speaking, but the voice was strong and deep. She had never heard a more beautiful voice.
"I know, Halvor, it doesn't seem reasonable to you that a poor, uneducated blacksmith should have found the truth, when so many learned men have failed," said the voice.
"I don't see how you can be so sure of that," Halvor said.
"It's Hellgum, talking to Halvor," Karin thought, trying to close the window, though she could not reach it.

"It's been said, as you know," Hellgum went on, "that if someone strikes us on one cheek we must turn the other, and that we shouldn't resist evil, and other things along those lines--none of which any of us can actually live by. Why, people would rob you of house and home, they'd steal your potatoes and carry off your grain, if you didn't protect what was yours. I suppose they'd take the whole Ingmar Farm from you."
"Maybe you're right," Halvor admitted.
"Well, then, I suppose Christ didn't mean anything by all that--just talking into thin air, was He?"
"I don't know what you're getting at," said Halvor.

"Now here's something to think about," Hellgum went on. "We're supposed to be very advanced in our Christianity nowadays. No one steals anymore, no one commits murder or wrongs the widow and the orphan, and of course no one hates or persecutes his neighbor anymore--it wouldn't even occur to any of us, with such a fine religion, to do wrong!"
"There are plenty of things that aren't quite as they should be," Halvor drawled, sounding sleepy and anything but interested.

"Now, if you had a threshing machine that wouldn't run, you'd find out what was wrong with it. You wouldn't rest until you'd figured out the flaw. But when you see it's simply impossible to get people to live a Christian life, shouldn't you try to find out whether something's wrong with Christianity itself?"
"I can't believe there's anything wrong with the teachings of Jesus," said Halvor.

"No, they were sound from the start, no question. But maybe they've grown a little rusty from neglect, so to speak. In any perfect machine, if one cog slips--just one tiny cog--the whole mechanism stops!"
He paused for a moment, as if searching for the right words and proof.

"Now let me tell you what happened to me a few years back," he went on. "I tried, for the first time in my life, to really live by the teachings. Do you know what came of it? I was working in a factory at the time. When my fellow workers found out what sort of man I was, they let me do a good share of their work along with my own. And how did they thank me? They conspired to pin the blame on me for a theft one of them had committed. I was arrested, of course, and sent to prison."
"You don't usually run into people that bad," Halvor answered, unmoved.

"Then I said to myself: it wouldn't be so hard to be a Christian if a person were alone on this earth, with no other people to deal with. I'll admit I actually enjoyed being in prison, since there I could lead a righteous life, undisturbed and unbothered. But after a while I began to think that trying to be good in isolation was about as useful as a mill turning by itself with no grain in the hopper. Since God had chosen to put so many people into the world,' I reasoned, 'it must have been meant for them to help and comfort one another, not threaten each other. It struck me, finally, that Satan must have taken something out of the Bible, so that Christianity would fall apart."
"Surely he never had the power to do that," said Halvor.
"He did--he removed this teaching: whoever wants to live a Christian life must seek help among his fellow men."
Halvor did not venture a reply, but Karin nodded in approval. She had been listening closely and had not missed a word.

"As soon as I got out of prison," Hellgum went on, "I went to see an old friend and asked him to help me live a righteous life. And mind you, the moment there were two of us at it, it got easier. Soon a third joined us, then a fourth, and it kept getting easier. Now there are thirty of us living together in a house in Chicago. All our interests are shared; we hold everything in common. We watch over each other's lives, and the path of righteousness lies smooth and even before us. We can deal with one another the way Christ would want, because no brother takes advantage of another's kindness, or tramples him down for his humility."

When Halvor said nothing, Hellgum pressed on persuasively: "You know, of course, that anyone who wants to accomplish something big always joins forces with others who can help him. You couldn't run this farm alone. If you wanted to start a factory, you'd have to form a company to work with you, and if you wanted to build a railway, just think how many hands you'd need to take on!"

"But the hardest work in the world is living a Christian life--and that, somehow, you're expected to manage single-handed, without anyone's support. Or maybe you don't even try, since you already know it can't be done alone. But we--I and the others who've joined me back in Chicago--have found a way. Our little community is truly the New Jerusalem come down from Heaven. You'll know it by these signs: the gifts of the Spirit that came down on the early Christians have come down on us too. Some of us hear the Voice of God, others prophesy, and others still heal the sick--"
"Can you heal the sick?" Halvor broke in eagerly.
"Yes," Hellgum answered. "I can heal those who have faith in me."
"It's hard to believe something so different from what you were taught as a child," Halvor said thoughtfully.
"Even so, I feel certain, Halvor, that very soon you'll give your full support to building up the New Jerusalem," Hellgum declared.
Then there was a moment of silence, after which Karin heard Hellgum say goodbye.
Presently Halvor came into the house. Seeing Karin sitting by the open window, he said, "You must have heard everything Hellgum said."
"Yes," she said.
"Did you hear him say he could heal anyone who has faith in him?"

Karin flushed a little. She had liked what Hellgum said better than anything she had heard all summer. There was something sound and practical in his teaching that appealed to her common sense. Here was action and service, not just feeling, which meant nothing to her. Still, she would not admit it, since she had made up her mind to have nothing more to do with preachers. So she told Halvor: "My father's faith is good enough for me."

A fortnight later Karin was again sitting in the living room. Autumn had just set in; the wind howled around the house and a fire crackled on the hearth. No one was in the room but herself and her baby daughter, who was nearly a year old and had just learned to walk. The child sat on the floor at her mother's feet, playing.
As Karin sat watching the child, the door opened and in came a tall, dark man with sharp eyes and big, sinewy hands. Before he said a word, Karin guessed it was Hellgum.

After exchanging greetings, the man asked after Halvor. He learned that Karin's husband had gone to a town meeting and was expected home soon. Hellgum sat down. Now and then he glanced at Karin, and after a while he said:
"I've been told you're ill."
"I haven't been able to walk for the past six months," Karin replied.
"I've been thinking of coming here to pray for you," the preacher offered.
Karin closed her eyes and withdrew into herself.
"You've perhaps heard that, by the grace of God, I'm able to heal the sick?"
The woman opened her eyes and gave him a look of distrust. "I'm grateful to you for thinking of me," she said, "but it isn't likely you can help me, since I'm not the sort who changes faith easily."
"Perhaps God will help you anyway, since you've always tried to live an upright life."
"I'm afraid I don't stand well enough with God to expect His help in this."
After a moment Hellgum asked if she had looked inward to find the cause of this affliction. "Has Mother Karin ever asked herself why this has been visited on her?"
Karin made no reply; once more she seemed to withdraw into herself.
"Something tells me God has done this so His name might be glorified," said Hellgum.
At that, Karin grew angry, and two bright red spots appeared on her cheeks. She thought it presumptuous of Hellgum to imagine that her illness had come upon her just so he could perform a miracle.
After a moment the preacher rose and went over to Karin. Laying his heavy hand on her head, he asked: "Do you want me to pray for you?"

Karin immediately felt a rush of life and health surge through her body, but she was so offended at his presumption that she pushed his hand away and raised her own as if to strike him. Her indignation was beyond words.
Hellgum withdrew toward the door. "One shouldn't refuse the help God sends, but accept it with thanks."
"That's true," Karin answered. "Whatever God sends, one has to accept."
"Mark my words! This very day, salvation shall come to this house," the man declared.
Karin didn't answer.
"Think of me when the help comes," he said. The next moment he was gone.

Karin sat bolt upright in her chair, the red spots still burning in her cheeks. "Am I to have no peace, even in my own house?" she muttered. "It's strange how many people nowadays think themselves sent by God."

Suddenly Karin's little girl got up and toddled toward the fireplace. The bright blaze had caught the child's eye, and she made for it as fast as her small feet could carry her, shrieking with delight.

Karin called for her to come back, but the child paid no attention; by then she was trying to climb up into the fireplace. After tumbling down a couple of times, she finally managed to get up onto the hearth, right where the fire was burning.
"God help me! God help me!" Karin cried. Then she began shouting for help, though she knew no one was near.

The little girl leaned laughing over the fire. Suddenly a burning ember rolled out and landed on her little yellow dress. Karin sprang instantly to her feet, rushed to the fireplace, and snatched the child into her arms. Not until she had brushed away every spark from the child's dress, and made sure the baby was unharmed, did she realize what had happened to herself. She was standing--she had been walking, and she would be able to walk from now on!

Karin felt the greatest shock she had ever experienced in her life, and at the same time the greatest happiness. She felt she was under God's special care and protection, and that God Himself had sent a holy man to her house to strengthen and heal her.

That autumn Hellgum often stood on the little porch of Strong Ingmar's cottage, gazing out over the countryside. The land grew more beautiful by the day: the ground had turned golden brown, and all the leafy trees had gone bright red or bright yellow. Here and there stretches of woodland shimmered in the breeze like a rolling sea of gold. Against the dark backdrop of the fir-covered hills, splashes of yellow stood out--leaf trees that had strayed in among the pines and spruces and taken root there.

The way a humble gray hut, once ablaze, gives off light and brilliance, so this humble Swedish landscape blazed into splendor. Everything was so wondrously golden, just as one might imagine a landscape on the surface of the sun would look.

Watching this, Hellgum was thinking that a time was coming when God would let the land reflect the brightness of His glory, and when the seeds of Truth sown that summer would yield golden harvests of righteousness.
Then, lo and behold, one evening Tims Halvor came over to the croft and invited Hellgum and his wife to come with him to the Ingmar Farm!

When they arrived, they found everything in holiday order. Around the house, all the old dry birch leaves had been swept away; the farm tools and carts, usually scattered across the yard, had been put out of sight.
"They must be expecting a number of guests," thought Anna Lisa. Just then Halvor opened the front door, and they went inside.

The living room was full of people, seated on benches all along the walls, waiting solemnly. Hellgum noticed they were the parish's leading people. The first he recognized were Ljung Bjoern Olofsson and his wife, Martha Ingmarsson, and also Bullet Gunner and his wife. Then he saw Krister Larsson and Israel Tomasson with their wives, all members of the Ingmar family. Presently he spotted Hoek Matts Ericsson and his son Gabriel, the councilman's daughter Gunhild, and several others besides. In all, about twenty people were present.
When Hellgum and Anna Lisa had gone around shaking everyone's hand, Tims Halvor spoke up:

"We who've gathered here have been thinking over what Hellgum has told us this summer. Most of us come from an old family that has always tried to walk in the ways of God. If Hellgum can help us do that, we're ready to follow him."
The next day, news spread like wildfire through the parish that a new religious sect had sprung up at the Ingmar Farm--one supposed to embody the only correct and true principles of Christianity.

chapters.title: Book Two — The New Way
paragraphs: In the spring, soon after the snow had melted, young Ingmar and Strong Ingmar came back to the village to start up the sawmill. They'd spent the whole winter up in the forest cutting timber and making charcoal. When Ingmar got back down to the lowlands, he felt like a bear just crawled out of its den. He could hardly get used to the glare of open sky, and blinked as if the light hurt him. The roar of the rapids and the sound of human voices seemed almost more than he could bear, and every noise on the farm was pure torture to his ears. And yet he was glad; heaven knows he didn't show it, in speech or manner, but that spring he felt as young as the fresh shoots on the birches.

Oh, but it felt good to sleep in a comfortable bed again, and to eat properly cooked food! And to be home with Karin, who fussed over his comfort as tenderly as a mother. She'd ordered him new clothes, and she had a habit of coming in from the kitchen to hand him some treat or other, as if he were still a little boy. And what wonderful things had happened at home while he was up in the forest! Ingmar had heard only a few vague rumors about Hellgum's teachings, but now Karin and Halvor told him about the great happiness that had come to them, and how they and their friends were trying to help each other walk in the ways of God.
"We're sure you'll want to join us," said Karin.
Ingmar said that maybe he would, but he wanted to think it over first.
"All winter I longed for you to come home and share our joy," the sister went on, "because now we no longer live on earth, but in 'the new Jerusalem which is come down from Heaven!'"

Ingmar said he was glad to hear Hellgum was still in the neighborhood. The summer before, the preacher had often dropped by the mill to chat with Ingmar, and the two had become good friends. Ingmar thought him the finest fellow he'd ever met. He'd never come across anyone so much of a man, so firm in his convictions, so sure of himself. Sometimes, when there was a big rush of work at the mill, Hellgum had pulled off his coat and pitched in. Ingmar had been amazed at the man's skill; he'd never seen anyone so quick at his work. Just then Hellgum happened to be away for a few days, but he was expected back soon.
"Once you've talked with Hellgum, I think you'll join us," Karin said. Ingmar thought so too, though he felt a little reluctant about accepting anything his father hadn't approved of.
"But wasn't it father himself who taught us that we must always walk in the ways of God?" Karin argued.

Everything seemed so bright, so promising! Ingmar had never dreamed it would feel this good to be back among people again. Only one thing was missing: no one ever spoke of the schoolmaster and his wife, or of Gertrude, and that troubled him. He hadn't seen Gertrude in a whole year. In the summer he'd never gone without news of her, since hardly a day went by that someone didn't mention the Storms. He told himself that maybe this silence about his old friends was just an accident. But when you feel too shy to ask, and no one brings up on their own the very thing you're longing to hear about, it's more than a little maddening.
But if young Ingmar seemed happy and content, the same couldn't be said of Strong Ingmar. Lately the old man had grown sullen, tight-lipped, and hard to get along with.
"I believe you're homesick for the forest," Ingmar said to him one afternoon as they sat on separate logs eating their sandwiches.
"God knows I am!" the old man burst out. "I only wish I'd never come back at all!"
"Why, what's gone wrong at home?"
"How can you ask! You must know as well as I do that Hellgum has been raising the devil around here."
Ingmar answered that, on the contrary, he'd heard Hellgum had become a big man.
"Yes, he's grown so big and strong that he's managed to turn the whole parish upside down," Strong Ingmar sneered.

It struck Ingmar as strange that the old man never showed a scrap of affection for anyone in his own family. He cared for nothing and no one except the Ingmarssons and the Ingmar farm. So Ingmar felt he had to stand up for his brother-in-law.
"I think his teaching is a good one," he said.
"Oh, you do, do you?" the old man snapped, giving him a withering look. "Do you think Big Ingmar would have thought so?"
Ingmar replied that his father would have stood behind anyone who worked for righteousness.

"So you believe Big Ingmar would have approved of calling everyone who doesn't belong to Hellgum's flock devils and antichrists, and would have refused to have anything to do with his old friends just because they kept the old faith?"
"I don't think people like Hellgum and Halvor and Karin would behave that way," said Ingmar.
"Just you try crossing them once, and you'll soon hear what they think of you!"
Ingmar bit off a big corner of his sandwich and stuffed his mouth full so he wouldn't have to talk. It irritated him to see Strong Ingmar in such a foul mood.

"Heigho, hum! It's a strange world," the old man sighed. "Here you sit, the son of Big Ingmar, with nothing to say for yourself, while my Anna Lisa and her husband are living off the fat of your land. The best people in the parish bow and scrape to them, and every day they're being feted, here, there, and everywhere."
Ingmar kept chewing and swallowing. There was nothing he could say to that. But Strong Ingmar came at him again.

"Yes, it's a fine doctrine Hellgum's spreading! That's why half the parish has gone over to him. No one has ever had such a hold on people, not even Strong Ingmar himself. He splits children from their parents by preaching that his flock mustn't live among sinners. Hellgum only has to crook his finger, and brother leaves brother, friend leaves friend, and a man deserts his own betrothed. He's used his power to sow strife and division in every household. Of course Big Ingmar would've been tickled to death by that! No doubt he would've backed Hellgum up in it all! I can just picture him doing it!"
Ingmar looked up and down; he wanted to get away. He knew well enough the old man had been laying it on thick, but the talk depressed him all the same.

"I won't deny that Hellgum has worked wonders," he allowed. "The way he keeps his people together, and gets folks who used to want nothing to do with each other living on friendly terms, is remarkable, no question. And look how he takes from the rich to give to the poor, and gets each one looking out for the other's welfare. I'm only sorry for the ones left outside, the ones called children of the devil who don't get to play. But of course you don't feel that way."
Ingmar was thoroughly annoyed with the old man for running Hellgum down like that.

"There used to be such peace and harmony in this parish!" the old man rattled on. "But that's all gone now. In Big Ingmar's day we lived in such unity that we were known as the friendliest people in all Dalecarlia. Now it's angels squaring off against devils, and sheep against goats."
"If we could only get the saws going," Ingmar thought, "I wouldn't have to listen to any more of this!"
"It won't be long now before it's all over between you and me, either," Strong Ingmar went on. "Because if you join Hellgum's angels, it isn't likely they'll let you keep company with me."

With an oath Ingmar jumped to his feet. "If you keep talking like that, it may turn out just the way you say," he warned. "You'd better understand, once and for all, that it's no use trying to turn me against my own people, or against Hellgum, who's the finest man I know."
That silenced the old man. After a while he left his work, saying he was going down to the village to see his friend Corporal Felt. He hadn't talked to a sensible person in a long time, he declared.
Ingmar was glad to see him go. Naturally, when a person's been away from home a long time, he doesn't want to hear unpleasant things; he wants everyone around him bright and cheerful.
At five the next morning Ingmar got down to the mill, but Strong Ingmar was already there ahead of him.
"Today you'll get to see Hellgum," the old man began. "He and Anna Lisa got back late last night. I expect they hurried home from their round of feasting just to convert you."

"So you're at it again!" Ingmar scowled. The old man's words had been ringing in his ears all night, and he couldn't help wondering who was in the right. But now he didn't want to hear any more talk against his relatives. The old man held his tongue for a while; then he began to chuckle.
"What are you laughing at?" Ingmar demanded, his hand on the sluice gate, ready to set the sawmill going.
"I was just thinking about the schoolmaster's Gertrude."
"What about her?"
"They were saying down at the village yesterday that she's the only one who has any influence over Hellgum--"
"What's Gertrude got to do with Hellgum?"

Ingmar, meanwhile, hadn't opened the sluice gate yet, since with the saws running he couldn't have heard a word. The old man eyed him questioningly. Ingmar smiled a little. "You always manage to get your own way somehow," he said.
"It was that silly goose, Gunhild, Councilman Clementsson's daughter, who--"
"She's no silly goose!" Ingmar broke in.

"Oh, call her whatever you like, but she happened to be at the Ingmar farm when this new sect was founded. The moment she got home, she told her parents she'd accepted the one true faith, and that she'd have to leave them and go live at the Ingmar farm. Her parents naturally asked why she wanted to leave home. So she could lead a righteous life, she told them straight out. But they figured that could be done just as well at home with them. Oh, no, that wouldn't work, she said, not unless she could live among people of the same faith. Then her father asked if all of them were planning to move to the Ingmar farm. No, just her; the others had true Christians right in their own homes. Now Clementsson is a decent sort, as you know, and both he and his wife tried reasoning with Gunhild as kindly as they could, but she wouldn't budge. Finally her father got so fed up that he just took her and locked her in her room, telling her she'd stay there till this crazy fit passed."
"I thought you were going to tell me about Gertrude," Ingmar reminded him.

"I'll get to her, if you'll just be patient. I might as well tell you right off that early the next morning, while Gertrude and Mother Stina were sitting in the kitchen spinning, Mrs. Clementsson came to see them. The moment they saw her they got worried. She was usually so cheerful and light-hearted, but now she looked like she'd cried her eyes out. 'What's wrong? What's happened? Why do you look so miserable?' they asked. Then Mother Clementsson answered that when a person's lost her dearest treasure, she can hardly be expected to look cheerful. I'd like to give them both a good beating!" said the old man.
"Who?" asked Ingmar.
"Why, Hellgum and Anna Lisa. They marched down to Clementsson's in the middle of the night and kidnapped Gunhild."
A cry of amazement escaped Ingmar.

"I'm starting to think my Anna Lisa is married to an outlaw!" said the old man. "In the dead of night they went and tapped on Gunhild's window and asked her why she wasn't at the Ingmar farm. She told them her parents had locked her in. 'It was Satan who made them do it,' said Hellgum. Her father and mother heard every word of it."
"Did they really?"
"Yes, they were sleeping in the next room, and the door between was standing partly open, so they heard everything Hellgum said to lure their daughter away."
"But they could have sent him packing."

"They felt Gunhild ought to decide for herself. How could they imagine she'd want to leave them, after all they'd done for her? They lay there expecting to hear her say she'd never desert her old parents."
"Did she go?"

"Yes, Hellgum wouldn't budge until the girl went along with them. Once Clementsson and his wife realized she couldn't resist Hellgum, they let her go. Some people are like that, you know. In the morning the mother regretted it, and begged the father to drive down to the Ingmar farm and bring their daughter back. 'No indeed!' he said. 'I'll do no such thing, and what's more, I never want to set eyes on her again unless she comes home of her own accord.' Then Mrs. Clementsson hurried down to the school to see if Gertrude wouldn't go talk to Gunhild."
"Did Gertrude go?"
"Yes. She tried to reason with Gunhild, but Gunhild wouldn't listen."
"I haven't seen Gunhild at our house," Ingmar said thoughtfully.

"No, because now she's back with her parents. Seems that when Gertrude left Gunhild, she ran into Hellgum. 'There stands the one who's to blame for all this,' she thought, and she marched straight up to him and gave him a tongue-lashing. She wouldn't have minded striking him, either."
"Oh, Gertrude can talk, all right," said Ingmar, approving.
"She told Hellgum he'd behaved like a heathen raider and not like a Christian preacher, skulking about like that in the night and carrying off a young girl."
"What did Hellgum say to that?"

"He stood quietly listening for a while, then said, meek as you please, that she was right, he'd acted in haste. And that afternoon he took Gunhild back to her parents and made everything right again."
Ingmar glanced up at the old man with a smile. "Gertrude is splendid," he said, "and Hellgum is a fine fellow, even if he's a little strange."
"So that's how you take it, is it? I figured you'd wonder why Hellgum gave in to Gertrude like that."
Ingmar didn't answer that.
After a moment's thought the old man started up again. "There are plenty in the village who want to know which side you're on."
"I don't see that it matters which party I belong to."

"Let me remind you of something," said the old man. "In this parish we're used to having someone we can look up to as a leader. But now that Big Ingmar is gone, and the schoolmaster has lost his hold on people, and the pastor, as you know, never had much of a hand at ruling anyone, they're running after Hellgum, and they'll keep following him just as long as you're content to stay in the background."
Ingmar's hands dropped; he looked worn out. "But I don't know who's in the right," he protested.

"The people are looking to you to deliver them from Hellgum. You can be sure we were spared plenty of unpleasantness by being away all winter. It must have been something dreadful at the start, before people got used to this converting craze and to being called devils and hellhounds. But the worst of all was when the converted children started preaching!"
"You don't mean to tell me the children were preaching too," Ingmar said doubtfully.

"Oh, yes!" the old man came back. "Hellgum told them they should serve the Lord instead of playing, so they set about converting their elders. They lay in wait along the roadside and pounced on innocent passersby with ravings like: 'Aren't you going to begin the fight against the devil? Are you going to keep on living in sin?'"
Young Ingmar didn't want to believe what Strong Ingmar was telling him. "Old man Felt must have put all that into your head," he concluded.

"By the way, this is what I wanted to tell you," said Strong Ingmar. "Felt is done for too! When I think that all this mischief was hatched right here on the Ingmar farm, I'm ashamed to look people in the face."
"Have they wronged Felt somehow?" asked Ingmar.
"It was the work of those youngsters, drat them! One evening, with nothing better to do, they got it into their heads to go convert Felt, since of course they'd heard he was a terrible sinner."
"But in the old days all the children were as afraid of Felt as they were of witches and trolls," Ingmar reminded him.

"Oh, these youngsters were scared too, but they must have set their hearts on doing something heroic. So one evening, as Felt sat stirring his supper porridge, they stormed his cabin. When they opened the door and saw the old corporal sitting by the fire, with his bristling mustache, his broken nose, and his bad eye, they were terrified, and two of the littlest ones ran off. The dozen or so who went in knelt in a circle around the old man and started singing and praying."
"And didn't he chase them out?" asked Ingmar.

"If only he had!" the old man sighed. "I don't know what got into the corporal. The poor wretch must have been sitting there brooding over the loneliness and misery of his old age. And I suppose it was because it was children who'd come to him. The fact that children had always been afraid of him must have weighed on the old man, and when he saw all those baby faces turned up at him, their eyes brimming with tears, he was helpless. The children were only waiting for him to lunge at them and hit them. Even as they kept on singing and praying, they were ready to bolt the second he moved. Presently a couple of them noticed Felt's face starting to twitch. 'Now he'll go for us,' they thought, and started to get up to run. But the old man blinked his one good eye, and a tear rolled down his cheek. 'Hallelujah!' the youngsters shouted, and now, like I already told you, it's all up with Felt. Now he does nothing but run around to meetings, fasting and praying, and imagining he hears the voice of God."
"I don't see anything so terrible in all that," said Ingmar. "Felt was drinking himself to death before the Hellgumists took him in hand."
"Well, you've got so many friends to lose that a little thing like this wouldn't bother you. No doubt you'd have been pleased if the children had managed to convert the schoolmaster."
"I can't picture those poor little kids trying to take on Storm!" Ingmar was dumbfounded. What Strong Ingmar had said about the parish being turned upside down must be true after all, he thought.
"But they did, though," Strong Ingmar replied. "One evening, as Storm sat in the classroom writing, a score of them came in and started preaching at him."
"And what did Storm do?" asked Ingmar, unable to keep from laughing.
"He was so astonished at first that he couldn't say or do a thing. But as luck would have it, Hellgum had shown up a few minutes earlier and was in the kitchen talking with Gertrude."
"Hellgum was with Gertrude?"

"Yes. Hellgum and Gertrude have been friends ever since the day he took her advice in that business with Gunhild. When Gertrude heard the racket in the schoolroom, she said: 'You're just in time to see something new, Hellgum. Seems the children are going to instruct the schoolmaster from now on.' Then Hellgum laughed, because he saw how ridiculous it was. He promptly drove the children out and put a stop to it."
Ingmar noticed the old man was watching him in a peculiar way; it was like a hunter looking at a wounded bear, wondering whether to give it another shot.
"I don't know what you expect of me," said Ingmar.
"What could I expect of you, who's only a boy! Why, you don't have a penny to your name. All you've got in the world is your two empty hands."
"I honestly believe you want me to throttle Hellgum!"
"They were saying down at the village that this would all blow over soon enough if you could just talk Hellgum into leaving these parts."
"Whenever a new religious sect springs up there's always strife and division," said Ingmar. "So this is nothing out of the ordinary."
"All the same, this would be a good way for you to show people what you're made of," the old man persisted.

Ingmar turned away and set the saws going. More than anything he would have liked to ask how Gertrude was getting on, and whether she'd already joined the Hellgumists, but he was too proud to let his fears show.

At eight o'clock he went home for breakfast. As usual, the table was heaped with tempting dishes, and both Halvor and Karin were especially warm toward him. Seeing them so kind and gentle, he couldn't believe a word of Strong Ingmar's chatter. His heart felt light again, and he was sure the old man had exaggerated everything. But after a while his worry over Gertrude came back, with such force that it killed his appetite, and he couldn't touch his food. Suddenly he turned to Karin and said, out of nowhere:
"Have you seen anything of the Storms lately?"
"No!" Karin replied stiffly. "I don't care to associate with such godless people."

That answer set Ingmar thinking. He wondered whether he'd better speak up or hold his tongue. If he spoke, it might end in a break with his family, but at the same time he didn't want them thinking he agreed with them on something so plainly wrong. "I've never seen a sign of godlessness in the schoolmaster's family," he said back. "And I lived with them for four years."

The very thought that had just crossed Ingmar's mind now came to Karin too. She also wondered whether she should speak or stay silent. But she felt she had to stick to the truth, even if it hurt Ingmar, so she said that if people wouldn't listen to the voice of God, one couldn't help but think them godless.
Then Halvor spoke up. "The question of the children is a serious one," he said. "They need to be given the right kind of upbringing."
"Storm has trained this whole parish, you included, Halvor," Ingmar reminded him.
"But he hasn't taught us how to live rightly," said Karin.
"Seems to me you've always tried to do that, Karin."

"Let me tell you what it was like, living by the old teaching. It was like trying to walk a round beam: one minute you were up, the next you were down. But when I let my fellow Christians take me by the hand and hold me steady, I can walk the straight and narrow path of righteousness without stumbling."
"I dare say," Ingmar smiled, "but that's too easy."
"Even so, it's difficult enough, but no longer impossible."
"But what about the Storms?"
"Those of us who belong took their children out of the school. We didn't want the children picking up any of the old teaching."
"What did the schoolmaster say to that?"
"He said it was against the law to take children out of school, and promptly sent a constable over to Israel Tomasson's and Krister Larsson's to fetch their children back."
"And now you're not on friendly terms with the Storms?"
"We simply keep to ourselves."
"Seems like you're at odds with everyone."
"We only keep away from those who'd tempt us into sin."
As the three of them went on talking, they lowered their voices. They were all wary of every word, sensing the conversation had turned painful.
"But I can give you greetings from Gertrude," said Karin, trying to sound more cheerful. "Hellgum had many talks with her over the winter. He says she means to join us this evening."
Ingmar's lips began to quiver. It was as if he'd gone about blindfolded all day, waiting to be shot, and now the shot had come, the bullet straight through his heart.

"So she wants to be one of you!" he murmured faintly. "So much can happen here while a person's off in the dark forest." It seemed to Ingmar that all this time Hellgum had been working his way into Gertrude's favor, laying snares to catch her. "But what's to become of me?" he asked suddenly, and there was a strange, helpless note in his voice.
"You must embrace our faith," Halvor said firmly. "Hellgum is back now, and if he talks to you just once, you'll soon be converted."
"But maybe I don't care to be converted!"
Halvor and Karin stared at Ingmar in speechless amazement.
"Maybe I don't want any faith but my father's."
"Don't say anything until you've had a talk with Hellgum," Karin begged.

"But if I don't join you, I suppose you won't want me staying under your roof?" said Ingmar, rising. When they didn't answer, it felt to him as if he'd suddenly been cut off from everything. Then he pulled himself together and set his jaw. "Now I want to know what you mean to do about the sawmill!" he demanded, thinking it best to settle the matter once and for all.
Halvor and Karin exchanged glances; both were afraid of committing themselves.
"You know, Ingmar, that no one in the world is dearer to us than you," said Halvor.
"Yes, yes, but what about the sawmill?" Ingmar pressed.
"The main thing is to get all your timber sawed."
At Halvor's evasive answer, Ingmar drew his own conclusions. "Maybe Hellgum wants to run the sawmill too?"
Karin and Halvor were thrown by Ingmar's flash of temper; ever since they'd told him about Gertrude, they couldn't seem to get through to him.
"Let Hellgum talk to you," Karin pleaded.
"Oh, I'll let him talk to me," said Ingmar, "but first I'd like to know just where I stand."
"Surely, Ingmar, you must know we wish you well!"
"But Hellgum's to get the sawmill?"

"We have to find some suitable work for Hellgum so he can stay in his own country. We've been thinking that maybe you and he could become business partners, provided you accept the one true faith. Hellgum is a good worker." This from Halvor.
"Since when have you been afraid to speak plainly, Halvor?" said Ingmar. "All I want to know is whether Hellgum's to have the sawmill."
"He'll have it if you resist God," Halvor declared.
"I'm obliged to you for telling me what a fine stroke of business it'd be for me to take up your faith."
"You know perfectly well that's not how it was meant," said Karin, reproving him.

"I understand exactly what you mean," Ingmar returned. "I'm to lose Gertrude and the sawmill and the old home, unless I go over to the Hellgumists." Then he turned suddenly and walked out of the house.

Once outside, it occurred to him that he might as well put an end to this suspense and find out at once where he stood with Gertrude. So he went straight down to the schoolhouse. When Ingmar opened the gate a light spring rain was falling. In the schoolmaster's beautiful garden everything had started sprouting and budding. The ground was greening so fast you could almost watch the grass grow. Gertrude was standing on the steps watching the rain, two big bird-cherry bushes, thick with newly sprung leaves, spreading their branches over her. Ingmar paused a moment, struck by how lovely and peaceful everything looked down here. Already he felt his unease easing. Gertrude hadn't yet noticed him. He closed the gate very gently, then walked toward her. When he was quite close he stopped and stared at her in wonder. The last time he'd seen her she was hardly more than a child, but in one short year she'd grown into a dignified and beautiful young woman. She was tall and slender now, and fully grown, her head set finely on a graceful neck; her skin was soft and fair, shading into a fresh pink at the cheeks; her eyes were deep and thoughtful, and her mouth, which once had played host to mischief and laughter, now showed only seriousness and a wistful longing.

Seeing Gertrude so changed brought Ingmar a feeling of pure happiness. A peaceful stillness settled over his whole being, as though he stood in the presence of something great and holy. It was all so beautiful that he wanted to fall on his knees and thank God.

But when Gertrude saw Ingmar, she suddenly stiffened, her eyebrows drew together, and a shadow of a wrinkle appeared between her eyes. He saw at once that she didn't like his being there, and it cut him to the quick. "They want to take her from me," he thought; "they've already taken her from me." The feeling of Sabbath peace vanished, and the old fear and worry came flooding back. Dropping all ceremony, he asked Gertrude if it was true that she meant to join Hellgum and his followers. She answered that it was. Then Ingmar asked whether she'd considered that the Hellgumists wouldn't let her associate with people who didn't think as they did. Gertrude answered quietly that she'd thought the matter over carefully.
"Do you have your father's and mother's consent?" asked Ingmar.
"No," she replied. "They don't know anything yet."
"But, Gertrude--"
"Hush, Ingmar! I have to do this to find peace. God is compelling me."
"No," he cried, "not God, but--"
Gertrude turned toward him suddenly.
Then Ingmar told her he would never join the Hellgumists. "If you go over to them, it will part us forever."
Gertrude looked at him as if to say she didn't see how that could concern her.
"Don't do it, Gertrude!" he begged.
"You mustn't think I'm acting rashly, because I've given this very serious thought."
"Then think it over once more before you act."
Gertrude turned from him, impatient.
"You should think of Hellgum's sake too," said Ingmar, his anger rising, seizing her by the arm.
She shook off his hand. "Are you out of your mind, Ingmar?" she gasped.
"Yes," he answered. "These doings of Hellgum's are driving me mad. They have to be stopped!"
"What has to be stopped?"
"You'll find out before long."
Gertrude shrugged.
"Goodbye, Gertrude!" he said, his voice choking. "And remember what I've told you. You'll never join the Hellgumists!"
"What do you mean to do, Ingmar?" the girl asked, starting to feel uneasy.
"Goodbye, Gertrude, and think over what I've said!" Ingmar shouted back, for by then he was halfway down the gravel walk.

Then he went on his way. "If only I were as wise as my father!" he thought. "But what can I do? I'm about to lose everything that's dearest to me, and I don't see any way to stop it." One thing, though, Ingmar was certain of: if all this misery was going to be forced on him, Hellgum wasn't going to walk away unscathed.

He went down to Strong Ingmar's cabin, hoping to find the preacher there. When he reached the door, he caught the sound of loud, angry voices. There seemed to be several visitors inside, so he turned back at once. As he walked away he heard a man say, in an angry voice: "We're three brothers who've come a long way to call you to account, John Hellgum, for what's become of our younger brother. Two years ago he went over to America and joined your community. The other day we got a letter saying he's lost his mind, brooding over your teaching."
Then Ingmar hurried away. Apparently there were others besides himself with a grievance against Hellgum, and all of them just as helpless.

He went down to the sawmill, which Strong Ingmar had already set going. Above the buzz of the saws and the roar of the rapids he heard a shriek, but he paid it no particular mind. He had no thought for anything except his fierce hatred of Hellgum. He was tallying up in his mind everything this man had robbed him of: Gertrude and Karin, his home, his business.
Again he seemed to hear a cry. It occurred to him that perhaps a quarrel had broken out between Hellgum and the strangers. "No harm done if they beat the life out of him," he thought.

Then he heard a loud shout for help. Ingmar dropped his work and went running up the hill.
