The closer he got to the hut, the plainer he could hear Hellgum's cries of distress, and by the time he reached the cabin it seemed as if the ground around it was shaking from the scuffling and struggling inside.

He cautiously opened the door and slipped in. Over against the wall stood Hellgum, defending himself with an axe. The three strangers--all big, powerful men--were going at him with clubs. They carried no guns, so it was plain they'd only meant to give Hellgum a sound beating. But since he'd put up such a fight, they were so enraged they now meant to kill him. They barely noticed Ingmar; to them he was nothing but a lanky boy who'd wandered in.

For a moment Ingmar stood quietly watching. To him it was like a dream, the kind where the thing you want most suddenly appears without your knowing where it came from or how. Now and then Hellgum cried out for help.
"Surely you can't think I'd be fool enough to help you!" Ingmar said to himself.

Suddenly one of the men dealt Hellgum a terrific blow to the head that made him drop the axe and fall to the floor. Then the others threw down their clubs, drew their knives, and threw themselves on him. In that instant a thought flashed through Ingmar's mind. There was an old saying about the men of his family, that every one of them was fated at some point in his life to do a shameful, wicked deed. Was it his turn now, he wondered?

All at once one of the attackers found himself in the grip of a pair of powerful arms that lifted him clean off his feet and threw him bodily out of the house; the second one barely had time to think of getting up before the same thing happened to him; and the third, who'd scrambled to his feet, got a blow that sent him headlong after the others.

After Ingmar had thrown them all out, he went and stood in the doorway. "Don't you want to come back?" he called out, laughing. He wouldn't have minded them going at him; testing his own strength was good sport.

The three brothers looked ready to renew the fight, when one of them shouted that they'd better clear out--he'd spotted a figure coming along the path behind the elms. Furious at not having finished Hellgum off, they turned to go, but one of them ran back, pounced on Ingmar, and stabbed him in the neck.
"That's for meddling in our business!" he shouted.
Ingmar sank down, and the man ran off with a taunting laugh.

A few minutes later Karin came along and found Ingmar sitting on the doorstep with a wound in his neck, and inside she found Hellgum, who by then had gotten back on his feet and was leaning against the wall, axe in hand, his face covered in blood. Karin hadn't seen the men fleeing; she assumed Ingmar was the one who'd attacked Hellgum and wounded him. She was so horrified her knees shook. "No, no," she thought, "it can't be that anyone in our family is a murderer." Then she remembered her mother's story. "That explains it," she muttered, and hurried past Ingmar to Hellgum.
"Ingmar first!" cried Hellgum.
"The murderer shouldn't be helped before his victim," said Karin.
"Ingmar first! Ingmar first!" Hellgum kept shouting. He was so worked up he raised his axe at her. "He fought off the men who tried to kill me and saved my life!" he said.
When Karin finally understood, and turned to help Ingmar, he was gone. She saw him staggering across the yard and ran after him, calling, "Ingmar! Ingmar!"
Ingmar went on without even turning his head. But she soon caught up with him. Putting her hand on his arm, she said:
"Stop, Ingmar, and let me bind up your wound!"

He shook off her hand and went on like a blind man, following neither road nor path. Blood from the open wound trickled down under his clothes into one of his shoes. With every step, blood was squeezed out of the shoe, leaving a red mark on the ground.
Karin followed him, wringing her hands. "Stop, Ingmar, stop!" she pleaded. "Where are you going? Stop, I say!"
Ingmar tramped on, straight into the woods, where there was no one to help him. Karin kept her eyes fixed on his shoe, oozing blood. Every second the footprints grew redder and redder.

"He's going into the forest to lie down and bleed to death!" Karin thought. "God bless you, Ingmar, for helping Hellgum!" she said gently. "It took a man's courage to do that, and a man's strength too!"

Ingmar tramped straight ahead, paying his sister no attention at all. Then Karin ran past him and planted herself in his way. He stepped around her without so much as a glance. "Go help Hellgum," he muttered.
"Let me explain, Ingmar! Halvor and I were so sorry for what we said to you this morning, and I was just on my way to tell Hellgum that, whichever way this turned out, you were to keep the sawmill."
"Now you can give it to Hellgum," was Ingmar's answer. He walked on, stumbling over stones and stumps.
Karin stayed close behind, doing her best to win him over. "Can't you forgive me for the mistake I made a moment ago, thinking you'd fought with Hellgum? I could hardly have thought otherwise."

"You were quick enough to believe your own brother a murderer," Ingmar shot back, without looking at her. He kept walking. Where he'd trampled the grass down, blood dripped from the blades as they sprang back up. It was only after Karin noticed the strange way Ingmar spoke Hellgum's name that she began to grasp how much he hated the preacher. At the same time she saw what a big thing he'd done.
"Everyone will be singing your praises for what you did today, Ingmar. It'll be known far and wide," she said. "You don't want to die and miss out on all the honor, do you?"

Ingmar laughed scornfully. Then he turned toward her a face gone pale and haggard. "Why don't you go home, Karin?" he said. "I know well enough who you'd rather be helping." His steps grew more and more unsteady, and now, everywhere he'd walked, there was an unbroken streak of blood on the ground.

Karin was nearly beside herself at the sight of all that blood. The deep love she'd always felt for Ingmar flared up with new force. Now she was proud of her brother, and thought him a sturdy branch of the good old family tree.

"Oh, Ingmar!" she cried. "You'll have to answer to God and to your fellow men if you go on spilling your life's blood like this. You know that if there's anything I can do to make you want to live, you only have to say so."
Ingmar stopped and put his arm around a tree trunk to hold himself up. Then, with a bitter laugh, he said: "Maybe you'll send Hellgum back to America?"

Karin stood looking down at the pool of blood forming around Ingmar's left foot, turning over in her mind what her brother wanted of her. Could it be that he expected her to leave the beautiful garden of paradise she'd lived in all winter, and go back to the wretched, sinful world she'd come out of?

Ingmar turned to face her squarely. His face had gone waxen, the skin drawn tight across his temples, his nose like that of a dead man. But his lower lip was set with a determination he'd never shown before, the line of his mouth sharply drawn. It didn't look like he'd soften his demand.
"I don't think Hellgum and I can live in the same parish," he said, "but it's clear enough that I'm the one who has to go."

"No," Karin cried quickly, "if you'll only let me take care of you, so your life is spared to us, I promise I'll see to it that Hellgum leaves. God will surely find us another shepherd," she thought, "but for now it seems best to let Ingmar have his way."

After she'd stopped the bleeding, she helped Ingmar home and put him to bed. He wasn't badly hurt. All he needed was to rest quietly for a few days. He lay in a room upstairs, and Karin tended him and watched over him like a baby.

The first day Ingmar was delirious, reliving over and over everything that had happened that morning. Karin soon realized that Hellgum and the sawmill weren't the only things weighing on him. By evening his mind had cleared and settled; then Karin said to him: "Someone wants to speak to you."
Ingmar said he felt too tired to talk to anyone.
"But I think this will do you good."

Right after, Gertrude came into the room. She looked quite grave and troubled. Ingmar had been fond of Gertrude even in the old days, when she was full of mischief and provoking, but back then something in him had always fought against that love. Now, though, Gertrude had come through a hard year of longing and unrest that had changed her so wonderfully that Ingmar felt an overwhelming longing to win her. When Gertrude came over to the bed, Ingmar put his hand up over his eyes.
"Don't you want to look at me?" she asked.
Ingmar shook his head. He was like a stubborn child.
"I only want to say a few words to you," said Gertrude.
"I suppose you've come to tell me you've joined the Hellgumists?"
Then Gertrude knelt down beside the bed and lifted his hand away from his eyes. "There's something you don't know, Ingmar," she whispered.
He looked at her questioningly but said nothing. Gertrude blushed and hesitated. Finally she said:
"Last year, just as you were leaving us, I'd begun to care for you--the right way."
Ingmar colored to the roots of his hair, and a look of joy came into his eyes, but at once he grew grave and wary again.
"I've missed you so much, Ingmar!" she murmured.
He smiled doubtfully, but patted her hand a little, in thanks for her wanting to be kind to him.
"And you never once came back to see me," she said, reproachful. "It was as if I no longer existed for you."
"I didn't want to see you again until I was a well-off man who could propose to you," said Ingmar, as if that were simply obvious.

"But I thought you'd forgotten me!" Gertrude's eyes welled up. "You don't know what a terrible year it's been. Hellgum has been very kind, and has tried to comfort me. He said my heart would find rest if I gave it wholly to God."
Ingmar now looked at her with a new hope kindling in his eyes.
"I was so frightened when you came this morning," she confessed. "I felt I couldn't resist you, and that the old struggle would start all over again."
Ingmar's face lit up.

"But this evening, when I heard you'd helped the one man you hated, I couldn't hold out any longer." Gertrude flushed scarlet. "I felt somehow that I didn't have the strength to do anything that would separate me from you." Then she bowed her head over Ingmar's hand and kissed it.

And it seemed to Ingmar as if great bells were ringing in a holy day. Within him reigned Sabbath peace and stillness, while love, honey-sweet, rested on his lips, filling his whole being with a blissful solace.
BOOK THREE

chapters.title: Book Three — Loss Of L'Univers
paragraphs: One foggy night in the summer of 1880—about two years before the schoolmaster built his mission house and Hellgum came back from America—the great French liner L'Univers was steaming across the Atlantic, bound from New York to Havre.
It was about four in the morning, and all the passengers, along with most of the crew, were asleep in their berths. The big decks were completely empty.

Just then, near daybreak, an old French sailor lay tossing and turning in his hammock, unable to rest. There was quite a sea running, and the ship's timbers creaked without letup, but that certainly wasn't what kept him from sleeping. He and his mates occupied a large but very low compartment between decks. It was lit by a couple of lanterns, so he could make out the gray hammocks hanging in close rows, slowly swaying back and forth with their sleeping occupants. Now and then a strong gust of wind swept in through one of the hatches, so searchingly cold and damp that it brought to his mind a vivid picture of the vast sea around him, rolling its grayish-green waves beneath its veil of mist.
"There's nothing like the sea!" thought the old sailor.

As he lay there thinking, everything around him suddenly went strangely still—he heard neither the churn of the propeller, nor the rattle of the rudder chains, nor the lap of the waves, nor the whistle of the wind, nor any other sound at all. It seemed to him the ship had suddenly gone to the bottom, and that he and his mates would never be shrouded or laid in coffins, but would have to hang there in their gray hammocks in the depths of the sea until Judgment Day.

He'd always dreaded the thought that he might end up in a watery grave, but now the idea pleased him. He was glad it was the moving, clear water covering him, and not the heavy, black, suffocating earth of the churchyard. "There's nothing like the sea," he thought again.

Then a troubling thought came to him. He wondered whether lying at the bottom of the ocean without having received Extreme Unction might be bad for his soul. He began to fear that his soul would never find its way up to Heaven.

Just then his eye caught a faint glimmer of light coming from the forecastle. He raised himself up and leaned over the side of his hammock to see what it was. Presently he saw two figures coming, each carrying a lit candle. He leaned still farther forward to make out who they were. The hammocks hung so close together and so near the floor that anyone wanting to move through the room without pushing or knocking into the sleepers would have to crawl on hands and knees. The old sailor wondered who could possibly be making their way through such a crowded space. He soon made out that they were two small acolytes, in surplice and cassock, each carrying a lit candle.

The sailor wasn't at all surprised. It seemed only natural that such small folk could walk under the hammocks carrying lit candles. "I wonder if there's a priest with them," he said to himself. At once he heard the tinkle of a little bell and saw someone following them. But it wasn't a priest—it was an old woman, not much bigger than the boys.
The old woman looked familiar. "It must be Mother," he thought. "I've never seen anyone as tiny as Mother, and surely no one but Mother could come along so softly and quietly without waking people."

He noticed his mother had on, over her black dress, a long white linen surplice trimmed with a wide border of lace, the kind priests wear. In her hand she held the big missal with the gold cross that he'd seen hundreds of times lying on the altar in the church back home.

The little acolytes set their candles down beside his hammock and knelt, each swinging a censer. The old sailor caught the sweet smell of burning incense, saw blue clouds rising, and heard the rhythmic click, click of the censer chains. Meanwhile his mother had opened the big book and was reading the prayers for the dead. Now it seemed good to him to be lying at the bottom of the sea—far better than being in the churchyard. He stretched out in the hammock, and for a long while he could hear his mother's voice murmuring Latin words. The incense smoke curled around him as he listened to the steady click, click of the swinging censers.
Then it all stopped. The acolytes picked up their candles and walked off, followed by his mother, who suddenly shut the book with a bang. He watched all three disappear beneath the gray hammocks.

The moment they were gone, the silence broke. He heard his comrades breathing, the timbers creaking, the wind whistling, and the waves swishing against the ship. Then he knew he was still among the living, and still on top of the sea.
"Jesu Maria! What can the meaning of what I've seen tonight be?" he asked himself.
Ten minutes later L'Univers was struck amidships. It felt as if the steamer had been cut clean in two.
"This is what I expected," thought the old sailor.

In the terrible confusion that followed, while the other sailors, only half awake, rolled out of their hammocks, he carefully dressed himself in his best clothes. He'd already had a foretaste of death, and it had been sweet and gentle, and it seemed to him that the sea had already claimed him as its own.

A little cabin boy was asleep in the deckhouse near the dining salon when the collision happened. Startled by the shock, he sat up in his bunk, half dazed, wondering what had happened. Just above his head was a small porthole, and he peered through it. All he could see was fog, and some shadowy gray shape that seemed to have sprung out of the fog. He thought he saw huge gray wings. A giant bird must have swooped down on the ship, he thought. The steamer rolled and heeled as the huge monster went at it with claws and beak and beating wings.

The little cabin boy thought he was going to die of fright. In a second he was wide awake. Then he realized that a large sailing ship had collided with the steamer. He saw great sails and a strange deck, where men in oilskin coats were rushing about in wild terror. The wind picked up, and the sails grew taut as drums. The masts bulged, and the yards snapped off with a series of cracks that sounded like pistol shots. A big three-master, which had sailed straight into L'Univers in the thick fog, had somehow gotten her bowsprit wedged into the liner's side and couldn't break free. The passenger steamer listed heavily, but her propellers kept right on turning, so now the two ships were moving along together.
"Lord God!" the cabin boy exclaimed as he rushed out on deck. "That poor boat has run into us, and now it's sure to sink!"

It never crossed his mind that the steamer herself might be in danger, big and fine as she was. The officers came hurrying up, but when they saw it was only a sailing vessel that had collided with their ship, they felt entirely safe, and with complete confidence set about getting the two vessels clear of each other.

The little cabin boy stood on deck bare-legged, his shirt fluttering in the wind, waving to the unlucky men on the sailing ship to come over to the steamer and save themselves. At first no one seemed to notice him, but presently a big man with a red beard started motioning to him.
"Come over here, boy!" the man shouted, running to the rail. "The steamer's sinking!"
The little boy had no intention whatsoever of going over to the sailing ship. He shouted as loudly as he could that the people on the doomed boat should come over to L'Univers and save their lives.

While the other men on the three-master worked with poles and boat hooks to free their ship from the steamer, the man with the red beard could think of nothing but the little cabin boy, for whom he'd clearly taken an extraordinary pity. He cupped his hands around his mouth like a trumpet and called, "Come over here, come over here!"

The little boy looked forlorn and cold, standing on deck in his thin shirt. He stamped his foot and shook his fist at the men on the other ship, angry that they wouldn't listen to him and come aboard the steamer. A great greyhound of a ship like L'Univers, with six hundred passengers and a crew of two hundred, couldn't possibly go down, he reasoned. And besides, he could see that the captain and the sailors were just as calm as he was.

Suddenly the man with the red beard grabbed a boat hook, thrust it out toward the boy, caught him by the shirt, and tried to pull him onto the other ship. The boy was dragged as far as the railing, but there he managed to free himself from the hook. He wasn't going to let himself be dragged over onto a strange ship that was doomed.

Right after that came another crash. The three-master's bowsprit had snapped, and the two ships were now clear of each other. As the liner steamed ahead, the boy saw the big broken bowsprit dangling from the other ship's bow, and he also saw great masses of sail drop down on the crew.

The liner kept on at full speed, and the sailing ship was soon lost to sight in the fog. The last thing the boy saw was the men struggling to get out from under the fallen sails. Then the ship vanished completely, as if it had slipped behind a great wall. "It's already gone down," the boy thought. And now he stood listening for cries of distress.
Then a rough, powerful voice came shouting across to the steamer: "Save your passengers! Put out your boats!"
Again there was silence, and again the boy listened for cries of distress. Then the voice came again, as if from far away: "Pray to God, for you are lost!"
Just then an old sailor stepped up to the captain. "We've got a big hole amidships. We're going down," he said, quietly and gravely.

Soon after word of the accident had spread through the steamer, a little lady appeared on deck. She had come from one of the first-class cabins, walking with a firm, determined step. She was dressed from head to foot, her bonnet strings tied in a neat bow. She was a small, elderly lady, with crimped hair, round owlish eyes, and a ruddy complexion.

In the short time the voyage had lasted, she'd managed to get acquainted with everyone aboard. Everybody knew her name was Miss Hoggs, and she'd told them all—crew and passengers alike—over and over, that she was never afraid. She didn't see why she should be, she'd said; she'd have to die sooner or later, and whether it happened soon or late made no difference to her. She wasn't afraid now, either. She'd come up on deck simply to see whether anything interesting or exciting was going on.

The first thing she saw was two sailors darting past with wild, terrified faces. Stewards, half dressed, came running out of their quarters to go wake the passengers and get them up on deck. An old sailor came up with an armful of life belts, which he dumped on the deck. A little cabin boy in his shirt was crouched in a corner, sobbing and shrieking that he was going to die. The captain was up on his bridge, and Miss Hoggs heard him order the engines stopped and the lifeboats manned.

Engineers and stokers came rushing up the grimy ladder from the engine room, shouting that the water had already reached the fires. Miss Hoggs had hardly been on deck a moment before it was crowded with steerage passengers, who had all come up together, shrieking that they'd better hurry and make for the boats, or only the first- and second-class passengers would be saved.

As the excitement and confusion grew, Miss Hoggs began to realize they were in real danger, so she quietly slipped away to the upper deck, where several lifeboats hung from their davits just outside the railing. There wasn't a soul up here, and, unseen, Miss Hoggs climbed over the railing and scrambled into one of the boats hanging above the watery abyss. Once safely inside, she congratulated herself on her foresight and good sense. That was the advantage of having a clear, cool head, she thought. She knew that once the boat was lowered there'd be a wild scramble for it; the crush in the gangway and on the companionway would be dreadful. Again and again she congratulated herself on having thought to get into the boat ahead of time.

Miss Hoggs's boat hung far aft, but by leaning over the edge she could see the companionway. She saw that one boat had been manned and people were climbing into it. Suddenly a terrible cry went up—someone had fallen overboard in the excitement. That must have frightened the others, because cries went up from all over the ship, and the passengers crowded heedlessly into the gangway, pushing and fighting their way toward the ladder. In the struggle, many of them went over the side. A few, seeing it was hopeless to reach the ladder, jumped straight into the sea, thinking they could swim to the boat. Just then the lifeboat, already loaded to capacity, rowed away. The people in it drew knives and threatened to cut off the fingers of anyone who tried to climb in.
Miss Hoggs saw one boat after another launched. She also saw one boat after another capsize under the weight of people throwing themselves down into them.
The lifeboats near hers were lowered, but for some reason no one had touched the one she was sitting in. "Thank God they're leaving my boat alone until the worst is over," she thought.

And Miss Hoggs heard and saw dreadful things. It felt to her as though she were suspended above hell itself. She couldn't see the deck itself, but from the sounds reaching her she could tell a frightful struggle was going on down there. She heard pistol shots and saw clouds of blue smoke rising into the air.

At last a moment came when everything went quiet. "Now would be the right time to lower my boat," thought Miss Hoggs. She wasn't the least bit afraid, and sat back with perfect composure until the steamer began to settle. Only then did it dawn on Miss Hoggs that L'Univers was sinking, and that her boat had been forgotten.

Among the passengers on the steamer was a young American matron, a Mrs. Gordon, on her way to Europe to visit her parents, who'd been living in Paris for some years. She had her two little boys with her, and all three were asleep in their cabin when the collision happened. The mother woke instantly, and managed to get the children partly dressed, then threw a cloak over her nightgown and went out into the narrow passageway between the cabins.

The passage was full of people who'd rushed out of their staterooms to hurry up on deck. Here it wasn't hard to get through, but in the companionway there was a terrible crush. She saw people pushing and crowding, thinking of no one but themselves, as more than a hundred of them all tried to rush up at once. The young American woman stood there holding her two children by the hand. She looked longingly up the stairway, wondering how she could possibly force her way through the crowd with her little ones. The people fought and struggled, thinking only of themselves. No one even noticed her.

Mrs. Gordon glanced around anxiously, hoping to find someone who would carry one of the boys up to the deck while she took the other. But she saw no one she dared approach. Men came dashing past, dressed every which way—some wrapped in blankets, others in overcoats thrown over their nightshirts, many of them carrying canes. Seeing the desperate look in these men's eyes, she felt it wouldn't be safe to speak to any of them.

Of the women, on the other hand, she wasn't afraid; but there wasn't one among them, either, to whom she'd dare entrust her child. They were all out of their minds with fear and couldn't have understood what she wanted of them. She stood watching them, wondering if there might be one, at least, with some reason left. But seeing them rush wildly past—some clutching the flowers they'd been given on leaving New York, others shrieking and wringing their hands—she knew it was useless to appeal to such frantic people. Finally she tried to stop a young man who'd been her table neighbor and had paid her marked attention.
"Oh, Mr. Martens—"
The man glared at her with the same fixed, savage stare she'd seen in the eyes of the other men. He raised his cane threateningly, and if she'd tried to hold him back, he would have struck her.

The next moment she heard a howl—though it was hardly a howl, more an angry murmur, like a strong sweeping wind bottled up in a narrow passage. It came from the people on the companionway, whose progress had suddenly been blocked.

A disabled man had been carried partway up the stairs—someone so completely helpless that he had to be carried to and from the table. He was a large, heavy man, and his valet had, with tremendous difficulty, managed to carry him on his back halfway up the stairs, where he'd stopped to catch his breath. Meanwhile the pressure from behind had grown so tremendous that it had forced the valet down onto his knees, and he and his master were now blocking the entire width of the stairway, an impassable obstruction.

Presently Mrs. Gordon saw a big, rough-looking man bend down, pick up the disabled man, and throw him over the banister. She also noticed that, horrible as this was, no one seemed shocked or moved by it. Nobody thought of anything but pushing ahead. It was as if a stone lying in the road had been picked up and tossed into the ditch—nothing more.
The young American mother saw that there was no hope of being saved among these people. She and her children were doomed.

There was a young bride and groom aboard, on their honeymoon. Their cabin was far down in the hull, and they'd slept so soundly they hadn't even heard the collision. There wasn't much commotion in their part of the ship afterward, either, and since no one had thought to wake them, they were still asleep while everyone else was up on deck fighting for the lifeboats. But they woke when the propeller, which had been turning directly under their heads all night, suddenly stopped. The husband hurriedly pulled on some clothes and ran out to see what was happening. A few minutes later he came back. He carefully shut the cabin door behind him before he said a word. Then he said:
"The ship is sinking."
At the same time he sat down, and when his wife started to rush out, he begged her to stay with him.

"The boats are all gone," he said. "Most of the passengers have drowned, and the ones still on board are up on deck now, fighting desperately for rafts and life belts." He told her that in the gangway he'd had to step over a woman who'd been trampled to death, and that he'd heard the cries of the doomed on every side. "There's no chance of our being saved, so don't go out! Let's die together!"
The young bride felt he was right, and sat down beside him in resignation.
"You wouldn't want to see all those people struggling and fighting," he said. "Since we have to die anyway, let's at least have a peaceful death."
She knew it was only right that she stay there with him for the few short moments of life left to them. Hadn't she promised him a whole lifetime of devotion?
"I had hoped," he went on, "that after we'd been married many, many years, you'd be sitting by me on my deathbed, and I could thank you for a long and happy life together."

Just then she saw a thin trickle of water seeping in through the crack under the door. That was too much for her. She threw up her arms in despair. "I can't!" she cried. "Let me go! I can't stay shut in here waiting for death. I love you, but I can't do it!"
She rushed out just as the ship heeled over, about to go down.

Young Mrs. Gordon was lying in the water. The steamer had sunk, her children were lost, and she herself had been dragged deep under the sea. She had come up to the surface for the third time now, and she knew that in another moment she'd be pulled under again, and that this time it would mean death.

Her mind no longer dwelt on her husband or children, or on anything else of this earth. She thought only of lifting her soul up to God. And her soul rose like a freed prisoner. Her spirit, rejoicing at the thought of casting off the heavy shackles of human existence, prepared joyfully to rise to its true home. "Is death really this easy?" she wondered.

As that thought came to her, the whole confused jumble of noises around her—the surging of the waves, the murmur of the wind, the shrieks of the drowning, the sounds of drifting wreckage colliding on the water—all seemed to resolve themselves into words, the way shapeless clouds sometimes form themselves into pictures. And this is what she heard:
"It's true that death is easy. Living—that's the hard thing!"
"Ah, so it is!" she thought, and wondered what it would take to make living as easy as dying.

All around her the shipwrecked people fought and struggled over the floating wreckage and the overturned boats. But amid the mad cries and curses, once again the noises resolved themselves into clear, powerful words:
"What is needed to make life as easy as death is UNITY, UNITY, UNITY."
It seemed to her that the Lord of all the earth had turned these noises into a speaking tube, through which He himself had answered her.

While those words were still ringing in her ears, she was rescued. She was hauled up into a small boat holding only three other people—a burly old sailor dressed in his best clothes, an elderly woman with round, owlish eyes, and a poor, heartbroken little boy wearing nothing but a torn shirt.

Late in the afternoon of the following day, a Norwegian ship sailed along the great banks of Newfoundland toward the fishing grounds. The sky was clear, and the sea lay like a mirror. The ship could make only slow headway. All her sails were set to catch the last breaths of the dying breeze.
The sea was very beautiful—a clear blue, smooth as glass, though wherever the faintest breeze passed over it, it turned silvery white.

After the afternoon stillness had gone on a while, the crew sighted a dark object floating on the water. It gradually drew nearer, and soon they made out that it was a human body. As the current carried it past the ship, they could tell from the clothing that it was a sailor. It lay on its back, eyes wide open, with a look of peace on its face. Clearly the body hadn't been in the water long enough to be disfigured. It was as if the sailor were placidly letting himself be rocked by the small rippling waves.

When the sailors looked the other way, they cried out. Before they could turn back, another body surfaced close to the bow. They very nearly ran it down, but at the last moment the swell washed it aside. Now they all rushed to the ship's rail and looked down. This time they saw the body of a child, a prettily dressed little girl. "Dear, dear," said the sailors, wiping their eyes. "The poor little thing!"

As the little girl's body drifted past, it seemed as though the child were looking up at them, and there was such a serious look in her wistful eyes, as if she were out on some very urgent errand. Right after that, one of the sailors shouted that he saw another body, and another man, looking the opposite way, said the same thing. All at once they saw five bodies, then ten, and then so many they couldn't count them.

The ship moved slowly on among all these dead people, who surrounded the vessel as if wanting something from her. Some drifted in large clusters, looking like driftwood carried out from land, but they were nothing but a mass of dead bodies.

The sailors stood aghast, afraid to move, hardly able to believe what they were seeing was real. All at once they seemed to see an island rising up out of the sea. From a distance it looked like land, but as they drew nearer they saw hundreds of bodies floating close together, surrounding the ship on every side. They moved along with the ship, as if wanting to make the crossing in her company. The skipper turned the rudder, trying to coax a little wind into the sails, but it didn't help much. The sails hung slack, and the dead kept following.

The sailors turned ashen, and silence fell over them. The ship had so little headway that she seemed unable to break free of the dead. They were afraid this might go on all night. Then a Swedish seaman stood up in the bow and recited the Lord's Prayer. After that he began singing a hymn. He was only halfway through it when the sun went down, and the evening breeze came up and carried the ship away from the region of the dead.

chapters.title: Book Three — Hellgum's Letter
paragraphs: An old woman came out of her little log cabin in the woods. Although it was only a weekday, she was dressed in her best, as if for church. After locking her door, she put the key in its usual spot, under the stoop.

When she'd gone a few paces, the old woman turned to look back at her cabin, which looked very small and very gray in the shadow of the towering snow-covered fir trees. She gazed at her humble home with fondness. "Many a happy day I've spent in that little old hut," she thought solemnly. "Ah, well. The Lord giveth, and the Lord taketh away."

Then she went on her way, down the forest road. She was very old and very frail, but she was one of those people who hold themselves upright and firm no matter how hard old age tries to bend them. She had a sweet face and soft white hair, and looked so mild and gentle that it came as a surprise to hear her speak in a voice as strident and solemn as some old-time evangelist's.

She had a long walk ahead of her, since she was going down to the Ingmar Farm for a meeting of the Hellgumists. Old Eva Gunnersdotter was one of the most zealous converts to Hellgum's teachings. "Ah, those were glorious times," she muttered to herself as she trudged along, "back at the start, when half the parish had gone over to Hellgum! Who would have thought so many would fall away, and that after five years there'd be barely twenty of us left—not counting the children, of course!"

Her thoughts went back to when she—having lived alone for so many years in the heart of the forest, forgotten by everyone—had suddenly found a whole crowd of brothers and sisters who came to her in her loneliness, who never forgot to clear a path to her cabin after a heavy snowfall, and who always kept her woodshed well stocked with dry firewood, all without her ever having to ask. She remembered the time when Karin, Ingmar's daughter, and her sisters, and many of the finest people in the parish, used to come and hold love feasts in her little gray cabin.

"Alas, that so many should have abandoned the one true way of salvation," she sighed. "Now retribution will come upon us. Next summer we must all perish, because so few of us have heeded the call, and because those who did hear it haven't stayed steadfast."

Then the old woman fell to thinking about Hellgum's letters—those letters the Hellgumists treated as apostolic writings and read aloud at every meeting, the way the Bible is read in churches. "There was a time when Hellgum was like milk and honey to us," she reflected. "Back then he told us to be kind and tolerant toward the unconverted, and to show gentle patience with those who'd fallen away. He taught the rich that in their charity they must treat the just and the unjust alike. But lately he's been like wormwood and gall. All he writes about now is trials and punishment."

By now she'd reached the edge of the forest, where she could look down over the village. It was a lovely day in February. The snow had spread its white purity over the whole district; all the trees lay deep in their winter sleep, and not a breath of wind stirred. But she was thinking that all this beautiful countryside, wrapped in peaceful slumber, would soon be woken only to be consumed in a rain of fire and brimstone. Everything now lying under its blanket of snow, she seemed to see wrapped in flame instead.

"He hasn't come right out and said it," the old woman thought, "but he keeps writing on and on about a sore trial. Mercy me! Who could wonder if this parish were punished like Sodom, and overthrown like Babylon!"

As Eva Gunnersdotter walked through the village, she couldn't look up at a single house without picturing how the coming earthquake would shake it apart and crumble it into dust and ashes. And whenever she met people along the way, she thought of how the monsters of hell would soon hunt them down and devour them.

"Ah, here comes the schoolmaster's Gertrude," she said to herself, seeing a pretty young girl coming down the road. "Her eyes sparkle like sunbeams on snow. She's happy now, expecting to marry young Ingmar Ingmarsson come fall. I see she's got a bundle of thread tucked under her arm—she's going to weave table covers and bed hangings for her new home. But before that weaving is finished, destruction will be upon us."

The old woman cast dark looks all around. She could see the village had grown and developed into something remarkably beautiful, but she thought all these pretty white-and-yellow houses, with their fancy gables and big bowed windows, would collapse just like her own humble gray cabin, where moss grew in the cracks between the logs and the windows were nothing but holes in the wall. When she reached the center of town, she stopped short and struck her cane hard against the pavement. A sudden fit of indignation had seized her. "Woe, woe!" she cried, so loudly that people in the street stopped and turned to look. "Yes—in all these houses live people who've rejected the Gospel of Christ and cling to the enemy's teaching. Why didn't they listen to the call and turn from their sins? It's on their account that we must all perish. God's hand strikes hard. It strikes the just and the unjust alike."

Once she'd crossed the river, some of the other Hellgumists caught up with her—Corporal Felt, and Bullet Gunner with his wife, Brita. Shortly after, they were joined by Hoek Matts Ericsson, his son Gabriel, and Gunhild, the daughter of Councilman Clementsson.

All these people, in their brightly colored national costumes, made a pretty picture walking along the snow-covered road. But to Eva Gunnersdotter's mind, they were nothing but doomed prisoners being marched to their execution, like cattle driven to slaughter.

The Hellgumists looked thoroughly downcast. They walked along with their eyes on the ground, as if weighed down by a terrible burden of discouragement. They'd all expected the Celestial Kingdom to spread suddenly over the whole earth, and that they'd live to see the day the New Jerusalem came down out of the clouds of heaven. But now that they'd dwindled to so few, and couldn't help seeing that theirs was a lost cause, something inside them seemed to have snapped. They moved slowly, dragging their feet. Now and then a sigh escaped one of them, but they seemed to have nothing to say to each other. This had been a matter of the utmost seriousness to them. They'd staked everything on it, and lost.

"Why do they look so down in the mouth?" the old woman wondered. "They don't seem to believe the worst, and they don't want to understand what Hellgum writes. I've tried to explain his words to them, but they won't even listen to me. Ah, well—people who live down in the open lowlands can never understand what it is to be afraid. They don't think the way we do, we who live alone in the dark forest."

She could tell the Hellgumists were uneasy because Halvor had called them together on a weekday. They were afraid he was going to tell them of more desertions from their ranks. They glanced anxiously at one another, with a look of distrust in their eyes that seemed to say: "How long will you hold out? And you—and you?"
"We might as well stop right now," they thought, "and break up the Society altogether. Sudden death would be easier, after all, than slowly wasting away."
How sad, that this little community with its gospel of peace, this blessed life of unity and brotherly love that had meant so much to all of them, should now be doomed.

As these disheartened people walked on toward the farm, the bright winter sun rolled cheerfully across the blue sky. A refreshing coolness rose from the glistening snow, which should have put life and courage into them, while from the fir-covered hills ringing the parish there fell a soothing peace and stillness.
At last they reached the Ingmar Farm.

In the farmhouse living room, up near the ceiling, hung an old painting done by some local artist a hundred years before their time. It showed a city surrounded by a high wall, above which rose the roofs and gables of many buildings—some of them red farmhouses with turf roofs, others white manor houses with slate roofs, and still others massive copper-plated towers like the one on the Kistine Church at Falun. Outside the city wall, gentlemen in knee breeches and buckled shoes strolled about carrying rattan canes. A coach could be seen driving out through the town gate, carrying ladies in powdered wigs and Watteau hats. Beyond the wall stood trees thick with dark green leaves, and on the ground, between patches of tall waving grass, ran little shimmering brooks. At the bottom of the picture, in large ornate letters, was painted: "This Is God's Holy City Jerusalem."
Hung as it was, so close to the ceiling, the old canvas rarely drew any notice. Most people who visited the Ingmar Farm didn't even know it was there.

But that day it was framed in a wreath of green whortleberry twigs, so it caught the eye at once. Eva Gunnersdotter noticed it right away, and murmured to herself: "Aha! So the folks at the Ingmar Farm know we must all perish. That's why they want us to turn our eyes toward the Heavenly City."
Karin and Halvor came forward to greet her, looking even gloomier and more low-spirited than the other Hellgumists. "It's plain they know now that the end is near," she thought.
Eva Gunnersdotter, being the oldest person present, was seated at the head of the long table. In front of her lay an opened letter, with American stamps on the envelope.
"Another letter has come from our dear brother Hellgum," said Halvor. "That's why I've called the brothers and sisters together."
"I take it you must think this a very important letter, Halvor," said Bullet Gunner thoughtfully.
"I do," Halvor replied. "Now we'll learn what Hellgum meant when he wrote in his last letter that a great trial of our faith lay ahead of us."
"I don't think any of us will be afraid to suffer for the Lord's cause," Gunner assured him.

Not all the Hellgumists had arrived yet, and there was a long wait before the last one finally appeared. Meanwhile old Eva Gunnersdotter, with her far-sighted eyes, sat gazing at Hellgum's letter. It made her think of the letter with the seven seals in Revelation, and she imagined that the moment any human hand touched it, the Angel of Destruction would come flying down from Heaven.

She raised her eyes and glanced up at the Jerusalem picture. "Yes, yes," she murmured, "of course I want to go to that city, whose gates are gold and whose walls are crystal!" And she began reciting to herself: "'And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald; the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.'"
The old woman was so absorbed in her beloved Book of Revelation that she gave a start, as if caught napping, when Halvor moved to the end of the table where the letter lay.
"We'll open the meeting with a hymn," Halvor announced. "Let's all join in singing number two hundred forty-four." And the Hellgumists sang together, "Jerusalem, My Happy Home."

Eva Gunnersdotter sighed with relief that the dreaded moment had been put off a little longer. "Dear me, that a doddering old woman like me should be so afraid to die," she thought, half ashamed of her own weakness.

When the hymn ended, Halvor picked up the letter and began unfolding it. At that, the Spirit moved Eva Gunnersdotter to rise and offer up a lengthy prayer for grace to receive its message in the right spirit. Halvor, letter in hand, stood quietly waiting until she'd finished. Then he began reading it in the tone he might have used delivering a sermon:
"My dear brothers and sisters, peace be with you.

"Until now I had thought that you and I, who have embraced my teaching, were alone in this faith of ours. But praise be to God—here in Chicago we have found brethren who are like-minded, who think and act according to these same principles.

"Know then that here in Chicago there lived, in the early eighties, a man named Edward Gordon. He and his wife were God-fearing people. It grieved them sorely to see so much distress in the world, and they prayed to God that grace might be given them to help those who sorrowed.

"It happened that Edward Gordon's wife had to make a long voyage across the sea, and she was shipwrecked and cast into the waters. When she found herself in the most extreme peril, the Voice of God spoke to her. And the Voice of God commanded her to teach mankind to live in unity.

"And the woman was saved from the sea and from the peril of death, and she came back to her husband and told him of the message from God. 'This is a great command our Lord has given us—that we live in unity—and we must follow it. So great is this message that in all the world there is only one place worthy of receiving it. Let us, then, gather our friends together and go with them to Jerusalem, so we may proclaim God's holy commandment from the Mount of Zion.'

"Then Edward Gordon and his wife, together with thirty others who wanted to obey the Lord's latest holy commandment, set out for Jerusalem, where they all now live together under one roof, in harmony. They share all their worldly goods with one another, and serve one another, each looking after the other's welfare.
"And they've taken the children of the poor into their home, and they nurse the sick, care for the aged, and help all who come to them for aid, expecting neither money nor gifts in return.
"But they don't preach in churches or on street corners, for they say, 'It is our works that shall speak for us.'

"But the people who heard of their way of life said of them, 'They must be fools and fanatics.' And the ones who cried out against them loudest were the Christians who had come to Palestine to convert Jews and Muslims by preaching and teaching. And they said, 'What sort of people are these, who don't preach? No doubt they've come here to lead sinful lives and indulge their lusts among the heathen.'

"And they raised such an outcry against these good people that it carried all the way back to their own country. Now, among those who had settled in Jerusalem was a rich widow with her two half-grown children. She had a brother back home, and everyone kept telling him, 'How can you let your sister live among those dreadful people, who lead such loose lives? They're nothing but idlers, living off her money.' So the brother began legal proceedings against his sister, to force her to send her children back to America to be raised there.
"And because of this legal action, the widow returned to Chicago with her children, accompanied by Edward Gordon and his wife. By then they had been living in Jerusalem fourteen years.
"When they returned from that far country, the newspapers had a great deal to say about them; some called them lunatics, and some said they were frauds."
When Halvor had read this far, he paused a moment, then repeated the substance of it in his own words, so everyone would understand it. Then he went on reading:
"Now, there is in Chicago a household you have heard of. Its members are people who try to serve God in spirit and in truth, who hold everything in common, and watch over one another's lives.

"We who live in this home read a newspaper piece about these 'lunatics' who'd come back from Jerusalem, and we said among ourselves, 'These people share our faith. They've banded together to work for righteousness, just as we have. We'd like to meet these people who share our ideals.'

"So we wrote and asked them to come see us, and those who had returned from Jerusalem accepted the invitation and visited. We compared our teachings with theirs and found our principles of faith were the same. 'It is by the grace of God that we have found one another,' we said.

"They told us of the glories of the Holy City, that city that lies resplendent on its white mountain, and we counted them fortunate to have had the privilege of walking the paths our Savior once walked.
"Then one of our own brethren said, 'Why shouldn't we go along with you to Jerusalem?'
"They answered, 'You mustn't come with us there, for God's Holy City is full of strife and discord, of want and sickness, of hate and poverty.'
"At once another of our brethren cried, 'Perhaps God has sent you to us because it is His will that we go with you to that far country, to help you fight against all this?'
"Then, every one of us, we heard the voice of the Spirit in our hearts say, 'Yes, this is My will!'
"Then we asked them whether they'd be willing to receive us into their fold, poor and unlettered as we were. And they answered that they would.

"So we resolved to become brethren in the fullest sense. They accepted our faith, and we theirs, and the whole while the Spirit was upon us, and we were filled with great gladness. And we said, 'Now we know that God loves us, since He sends us to that land where He once sent His own Son. And now we know our teaching is the true teaching, since God wants it proclaimed from His holy mountain Zion.'

"Then a third member of our household said, 'And there are our brothers and sisters back home in Sweden.' So we told the brethren from Jerusalem that there were more of us than they saw here, that we had brothers and sisters in Sweden too. We said, 'They are sorely tried in their fight for righteousness. Many have fallen away, and the few who've stayed steadfast are forced to live among unbelievers.'
"Then the travelers from Jerusalem answered, 'Let your brothers and sisters in Sweden follow us to Jerusalem, and share in our holy work.'

"At first we were glad at the thought of your following us and living with us at Jerusalem in peace and harmony. But afterward we grew troubled, and said, 'They will never leave their fine farms and their old occupations.'
"And the Jerusalem travelers answered, 'We cannot offer them fields and meadows, but they will be permitted to walk the paths where Jesus' own feet once trod.'
"But we were still doubtful, and said to them, 'They will never travel to a strange land where no one understands their speech.'
"And the travelers from Jerusalem answered, 'They will understand what the stones of Palestine have to tell them about their Savior.'
"We said, 'They will never divide their property among strangers and become poor as beggars, nor will they give up their authority, for they are the leading people of their own parish.'
"The travelers from Jerusalem answered, 'We have neither power nor worldly wealth to offer them, but we invite them to become participants in the sufferings of Christ their Redeemer.'

"When that was said, we were once again filled with gladness, and felt certain you would come. And now, my dear brothers and sisters, when you have read this, do not discuss it among yourselves, but be still and listen. And whatever the Spirit bids you do, do it."
Halvor folded the letter and said, "Now we must do as Hellgum writes. We must be still, and listen."
A long silence fell over the living room at the Ingmar Farm.

Old Eva Gunnersdotter sat as silent as the rest, waiting for the Voice of God to speak to her. She interpreted it all in her own way. "Why, of course," she thought, "Hellgum wants us to go to Jerusalem so we may escape the great destruction. The Lord means to save us from the flood of brimstone and keep us from the rain of fire, and those of us who are righteous will hear the Voice of God warning us to flee the wrath to come."

It never once occurred to the old woman that it might be a sacrifice for anyone to leave home and native land, when a matter like this was at stake. It never crossed her mind that anyone could doubt the wisdom of leaving behind his native woodlands, his smiling river, his fertile fields. Some of the Hellgumists thought with fear and dread of having to change their whole way of life, of giving up fatherland, parents, friends, and relatives; but not her. To her it simply meant that God wanted to spare them, as He'd once spared Noah and Lot. Weren't they being called to a life of supreme glory in God's Holy City? To her it was as though Hellgum had written that they'd be taken up bodily into heaven, like the prophet Elijah.

They all sat with their eyes closed, deep in meditation. Some were suffering such intense mental anguish that a cold sweat broke out on their foreheads. "Ah, this truly is the trial Hellgum foretold," they sighed.

The sun sat low on the horizon now, shooting its sharp rays into the room. The crimson glow of the setting sun cast a blood-red glare over the many pale faces. At last Martha Ingmarsson, wife of Ljung Bjoern Olofsson, slid down off her chair onto her knees. Then, one by one, the others all knelt too. All at once several of them drew a deep breath, and smiles lit up their faces.
Then Karin, Ingmar's daughter, said in a tone of wonder: "I hear God's voice calling me!"
Gunhild, Councillor Clementsson's daughter, lifted her hands in ecstasy, tears streaming down her face. "I'm going too," she cried. "God's voice calls me."
Then Krister Larsson and his wife said, almost in the same breath: "It cries in my ear that I must go. I can hear God's voice calling me!"

The call came to one after another, and with it all their mental anguish and every feeling of regret vanished. A great sense of joy came over them. They no longer thought of their farms or their relatives; they thought only of how their little colony would grow and blossom anew, and of the wonder of having been called to the Holy City.

The call had come now to most of them. But it hadn't yet reached Halvor Halvorsson. He was wrestling in anguished prayer, thinking God wouldn't call him the way He'd called the others. "He sees that I love my fields and meadows more than His word," he said to himself. "I am unworthy."
Karin went over to Halvor and laid her hand on his forehead. "You must be still, Halvor, and listen in silence."
Halvor wrung his hands so hard the joints of his fingers cracked. "Perhaps God doesn't consider me worthy to go," he said.
"Yes, Halvor, you'll be allowed to go, but you must be still," said Karin. She knelt down beside him and put her arm around him. "Now listen quietly, Halvor, and without fear."
In a few moments the tense look left his face. "I hear—I hear something, far, far away," he whispered.
"It's the harps of angels, announcing the presence of the Lord," his wife said. "Be very still now, Halvor." Then she pressed close against him—something she'd never done before in front of others.
"Ah!" he exclaimed, clapping his hands. "Now I've heard it. It spoke so loudly it was like thunder in my ears. 'You shall go to my Holy City, Jerusalem,' it said. Did you all hear it the same way?"
"Yes, yes," they cried, "we've all heard it."

But now old Eva Gunnersdotter began to wail. "I've heard nothing. I can't go with you. I'm like Lot's wife—I'm not allowed to flee the coming wrath, but must be left behind. Here I must stay, and be turned into a pillar of salt."

She wept in despair, and the Hellgumists all gathered around to pray with her. Still she heard nothing. And her despair turned into something like terror. "I can't hear anything!" she groaned. "But you've got to take me with you! You shan't leave me to perish in the lake of fire!"
"You must wait, Eva," said the Hellgumists. "The call may still come. It's sure to come, either tonight or in the morning."
"You're not answering me," cried the old woman. "You won't tell me what I want to know. Maybe you don't mean to take me with you if the call never comes to me!"
"It will come, it will come!" the Hellgumists shouted.
"You're not answering me!" the old woman screamed in a frenzy.
"Dear Eva, we can't take you along if God doesn't call you!" the Hellgumists protested. "But the call will come, never fear."

Then the old woman suddenly rose up from her knees, straightened her rickety old body, and brought her cane down on the floor with a thud. "You people mean to go away and leave me to perish!" she thundered. "Yes, yes, yes, you mean to go and let me perish!" She'd worked herself into a fury, and once again they saw before them the Eva Gunnersdotter of her younger days—strong, passionate, and fiery.

"I want nothing more to do with you!" she shrieked. "I don't want you to save me. Shame on you! You'd abandon wife and child, father and mother, just to save yourselves. Shame! You're a pack of fools, leaving your good farms behind. You're a lot of misguided idiots chasing after false prophets, that's what you are! It's you who'll have fire and brimstone rain down on you. It's you who must perish. But we who stay home—we shall live."

chapters.title: Book Three — The Big Log
paragraphs: At dusk, on that same beautiful February day, two young lovers stood talking together in the road. The young man had just driven down from the forest with a big log, so heavy the horse could hardly pull it. Even so, he'd taken a roundabout way so the log would be hauled through the village and past the big white schoolhouse.

The horse had been stopped in front of the school, and a young woman had come out to have a look at the log. She couldn't say enough in its praise—how long and thick it was, how straight, what lovely tan bark it had, how firm the wood was, and how flawless!

The young man told her, very impressively, that it had grown on a moor far north of Olaf's Peak, and just when he'd felled it, and how long it had been lying in the forest to dry out. He told her exactly how many inches it measured, both in circumference and diameter.
"But, Ingmar," she said, "it's only the first one!"

Pleased as she was, the thought that it had taken Ingmar five years to get down just this first bit of timber for their new home made her uneasy. But Ingmar seemed to think all the difficulties were behind them now.
"Just you wait, Gertrude!" he said. "If I can only get the timber hauled while the roads are still passable, we'll have the house up in no time."

It was turning bitterly cold. The horse stood there shivering all over, shaking its head and stamping its hooves, its mane and forelock white with hoarfrost. But the young man and the girl didn't feel the cold. They kept themselves warm building their house in their imaginations, from cellar to attic. Once they'd finished building it, they set about furnishing it.
"We'll put the sofa against the long wall here, in the living room," Ingmar decided.
"But I don't know that we have a sofa," said Gertrude.
The young man bit his lip. He hadn't meant to tell her until later that he already had a sofa waiting at the cabinetmaker's shop, but now he'd let the secret slip out without meaning to.

Then Gertrude came out with something she'd been keeping from him for five years, too. She told him she'd made hair ornaments and woven fancy ribbons to sell, and with the money she'd earned that way she'd bought all sorts of household things—pots and pans, platters and dishes, sheets and pillowcases, table covers and rugs.

Ingmar was so pleased with what Gertrude had done that he couldn't seem to praise her enough. In the middle of his praise he broke off suddenly and just gazed at her in speechless adoration. It seemed too good to be true that something so sweet and so beautiful would one day be his very own.
"Why are you looking at me so strangely?" asked the girl.
"I'm just thinking that the best part of it all is that you'll be mine."

Gertrude couldn't say a word, but she ran her hand tenderly over the big log that would form part of the wall of the house where she and Ingmar were going to live. She felt that protection and love awaited her there, for the man she was going to marry was good and wise, noble and faithful.

Just then an old woman passed by. She walked quickly, muttering to herself, as though furious about something: "Aye, aye, their happiness shall last no longer than from daybreak to rosy dawn. When the trial comes, their faith will snap like a rope spun from moss, and their lives will become one long darkness."
"Surely she can't mean us!" said the young girl.
"How could that possibly apply to us?" laughed the young man.

chapters.title: Book Three — The Ingmar Farm
paragraphs: It was the day after the Hellgumists' meeting, a Saturday. A blizzard was raging. The pastor, who'd been called to the bedside of a sick person living way up at the north end of the great forest, was driving home late that evening under terrible conditions. His horse sank deep into the snowdrifts, and the sledge kept threatening to tip over. Both the pastor and his hired man had to keep getting out to kick a path clear through the snow. Luckily it wasn't very dark—the moon kept rolling out from behind the snow clouds, big and full, spreading its silvery light over the ground. Glancing up, the pastor noticed the air was thick with whirling, flying snowflakes.

In some places they made their way easily enough. There were short stretches where the blowing snow hadn't settled, and others where the snow was deep but loose and even. The real trouble was getting over the places where the drifts were piled so high you couldn't even see over them, forcing them off the road to drive across fields and hedges, at the risk of being dumped into a ditch or having the horse impaled on a fence rail.

Both the pastor and his hired man spoke anxiously about the drift that always banked up against a high fence near the Ingmar Farm after a heavy snowfall. "If we can just get past that one, we're as good as home," they said.

The pastor remembered how often he'd asked Big Ingmar to take down that high fence, since it was the cause of so much snow drifting to that spot. But nothing had ever been done about it. Even though everything else at the Ingmar Farm had changed over the years, those old boards, at least, were never touched.

At last the farm came into sight. And sure enough, there was the snowdrift in its usual spot, high as a wall and hard as rock! There was no turning aside here—they had no choice but to drive straight over it. It looked impossible, so the hired man asked whether he shouldn't go down to the farm for help. But the pastor wouldn't hear of it. He hadn't exchanged a word with either Karin or Halvor in more than five years, and the thought of meeting old friends he was no longer on speaking terms with was no more pleasant to him than it would be to most people.

So the horse had to climb the drift. The icy crust held until the animal reached the top, then it gave way, and the horse suddenly vanished from sight as if into a grave, while the two men sat there staring down helplessly. One of the traces had snapped, so they couldn't have gone any farther even if they'd managed to get the horse out of the drift.

A few minutes later the pastor stepped into the living room at the Ingmar Farm. A blazing log fire burned on the hearth. The housewife sat on one side of the fireplace spinning fine carded wool, with the maids seated behind her in a long row, spinning flax. The men had claimed the other side of the fireplace. They'd just come in from their work; some were resting, while others, to pass the time, had taken up some light task—whittling sticks, sharpening rakes, making axe handles.

When the pastor described his mishap, everyone sprang into action, and the farmhands went out to dig the horse from the drift. Halvor led the pastor to the table and asked him to sit down. Karin sent the maids into the kitchen to make fresh coffee and prepare a special supper. Then she took the pastor's big fur coat and hung it by the fire to dry, lit the hanging lamp, and moved her spinning wheel up to the table so she could talk with the men.
"I couldn't have had a better welcome if Big Ingmar himself were still alive," thought the pastor.

Halvor talked at length about the weather and the state of the roads, then asked the pastor whether he'd gotten a good price for his grain, and whether he'd managed to get certain repairs done that he'd been wanting for so long. Karin then asked after the pastor's wife, and hoped there'd been some improvement in her health lately.

Just then the pastor's hired man came in to report that the horse had been dug out, the trace mended, and everything was ready to go. But Karin and Halvor pressed the pastor to stay for supper, and wouldn't take no for an answer.

The coffee tray was brought in, with the large silver coffee urn and the precious old silver sugar bowl on it—the bowl was never brought out except for grand occasions like weddings and funerals—along with three big silver cake baskets full of fresh rusks and cookies.
The pastor's small round eyes grew wide with astonishment. He sat as if in a trance, afraid of being woken from it.

Halvor showed the pastor the hide of an elk that had been shot in the woods on the Ingmar Farm. They spread the hide out on the floor, and the pastor declared he'd never seen a larger or more beautiful one. Then Karin went over to Halvor and whispered in his ear. At once Halvor turned to the pastor and asked him to accept the hide as a gift.

Karin bustled back and forth between the table and the cupboard, bringing out some choice old silverware. She'd spread a fine hemstitched cloth on the table and was setting it as though for a grand party, pouring milk and small beer into huge silver jugs.

When supper was over, the pastor excused himself and rose to leave. Halvor Halvorsson and two of his hired men went with him to clear a way through the drifts, steadying the sledge whenever it threatened to tip, and staying with him until he was safely inside his own dooryard.

The pastor was thinking how pleasant it was to renew old friendships as he said a hearty goodbye to Halvor. Halvor stood there feeling around in his pocket, and presently pulled out a folded slip of paper. He wondered if the pastor would mind taking it now—it was an announcement to be read after the morning service. If the pastor would be good enough to take it, it would save him the trouble of sending it to the church by special messenger.
Once the pastor was inside his house, he lit the lamp, unfolded the paper, and read:
"Owing to the owner's planned removal to Jerusalem, the Ingmar Farm is offered for sale—"
He read no further. "Well, well, so it's finally come upon us," he murmured, as if speaking of an approaching storm. "This is just what I've been expecting for years and years!"

chapters.title: Book Three — Hoek Matts Ericsson
paragraphs: It was a beautiful spring day. A farmer and his son were on their way to the great ironworks near the southern edge of the parish. Since they lived up at the north end, they had to travel almost the whole length of the parish. They passed newly sown fields, where the grain was just beginning to come up. They saw all the green rye fields and all the fine meadows, where the clover would soon be turning red and sending out its sweet scent.

They also passed a number of houses being repainted and fitted out with new windows and glassed-in verandas, and gardens where people were digging and planting. Everyone they met along the way had muddy shoes and dirty hands from working in the fields and vegetable gardens, planting potatoes, setting out cabbages, and sowing turnips and carrots.

The farmer simply had to stop and ask what kind of potatoes they were planting, and just when they'd sown their oats. At the sight of a calf or a foal, he'd immediately start figuring out how old it was. He calculated how many cows such-and-such a farm was likely to keep, and wondered how much this or that colt would fetch once it was broken.
The son tried again and again to turn his father's thoughts away from such things. "I'm thinking that you and I will soon be wandering through the valley of Sharon and the desert of Judea," he said.

The father smiled, his face brightening for a moment. "It will indeed be a blessed privilege to walk in the footsteps of our dear Lord Jesus," he answered. But the next minute, catching sight of a couple of cartloads of quicklime, his thoughts wandered off again. "Say, Gabriel, who do you suppose is hauling lime? They say lime makes for a rich crop as fertilizer. That'll be a sight for sore eyes come fall."
"In the fall, Father!" the son said reproachfully.
"Yes, I know," the farmer answered. "By fall I'll be dwelling in the tents of Jacob and laboring in the Lord's vineyard."
"Amen!" cried the son. "So be it. Amen!"

Then they walked on in silence for a while, watching the signs of spring. Water trickled in the ditches, and the road itself was badly rutted from the spring rains. Wherever they looked there was work to be done. Everyone felt the urge to pitch in and help, even when crossing a field that wasn't their own.

"To tell the truth," the farmer said thoughtfully, "I wish I'd sold the place in the fall, once the work was done. It's hard to leave it all behind in spring, just when you'd like to dig in with everything you've got."
The son only shrugged. He knew he'd have to let the old man talk.

"It's just thirty-one years now since I, as a young man, bought a piece of wasteland on the north side of this parish," the farmer said. "The ground had never once been touched by a spade. Half of it was bog, the other half nothing but stones. It looked pretty hopeless. On that very land I worked like a slave, digging up stones until my back was ready to break. But I think I worked even harder on that swamp, before I finally got it drained and filled in."
"Yes, you've certainly worked hard, Father," the son admitted. "That's exactly why God is mindful of you, and calls you to His Holy Land."

"At first," the farmer went on, "I lived in a shack not much better than a charcoal burner's hut. It was built of unstripped logs, with nothing but sod for a roof. I could never get it watertight, so the rain always came in. It was mighty uncomfortable, especially at night. The cow and the horse fared no better than I did—that whole first winter, they were kept in a mud cave as dark as a cellar."
"Father, how can you be so attached to a place where you've suffered such hardship?"

"But just think of the joy of it, when I was finally able to build a big barn for the animals, and how year after year my livestock grew, until I was forever having to add new wings to house them all. If I weren't selling the place now, I'd have to put a new roof on that barn. This would've been just the right time to do it—right after finishing the sowing."
"Father, you're to do your sowing in that land where some seed falls among thorns, some on stony ground, some by the wayside, and some on good ground."

"And the old cottage," the farmer went on, "the one I built after that first hut—I'd been meaning to tear it down this year and put up a fine new house. What's to become now of all the timber the two of us hauled home this winter? It was mighty hard work getting it down. The horses were driven hard, and so were we."

The son began to feel troubled. He thought his father was slipping away from him, afraid the old man wasn't offering up his property to the Lord in the right spirit. "Well," he argued, "but what are new houses and barns compared to the blessed privilege of living a pure life among people who are of one mind?"

"Hallelujah!" cried the father. "Don't you think I know a wonderful portion has been allotted to us? Aren't I on my way to the works right now, to sell my property to the Company? By the time I come back this way, it will all be gone, and I won't have a thing left I can call my own."
The son didn't answer, but he was glad to hear his father still held to his decision.
Presently they came to a farm beautifully set on a hill. There stood a white-painted house with a balcony and a veranda, and around it grew tall poplars, their pretty silvery trunks swollen with sap.

"Look!" said the farmer. "That's just the kind of house I meant to build—with a veranda and a balcony and plenty of ornamental woodwork, and a lawn out front mowed just like that one. Wouldn't that have been nice, Gabriel?"

Since the son said nothing, the farmer decided he must be tired of hearing about the farm, so he fell silent too, though his thoughts were still on his home. He wondered how the horses would fare with their new owners, and how things in general would be run on the place. "My goodness," he muttered under his breath, "I must be doing a foolish thing, selling out to a corporation! They'll go and cut down all the trees and let the farm run to waste. It'd be just like them to let the land turn marshy again, and let the birch woods creep back down into the fields."

They'd reached the ironworks at last, and the farmer's interest picked up again. There he saw plows and harrows of the latest design, and it suddenly reminded him that he'd been thinking for a long while about getting a new reaper. Gazing fondly at his handsome son, he pictured him sitting on a fine, red-painted reaper, cracking his whip over the horses, mowing down the thick, waving grass the way a war hero mows down his enemies. And as he stepped into the office, he seemed to hear the click of the reaper, the soft swish of falling grass, and the shrill chirp and quick flutter of startled birds and insects.
On the desk inside lay the deed. The negotiations were finished, and the price had been settled; all that remained to complete the deal was his signature.

While the deed was read out to him, he sat quietly listening. He heard that there were so many acres of woodland, so many of arable land and meadow, so many head of cattle, and such-and-such household furnishings, all of which he had to hand over. His face grew set.
"No," he said to himself, "it mustn't happen."
After the reading he was about to say he'd changed his mind, when his son leaned down and whispered to him:
"Father, it's a choice between me and the farm, because I'm going regardless of what you do."

The farmer had been so wrapped up in thoughts of his farm that it hadn't occurred to him his son might leave him. So Gabriel would go regardless! He couldn't quite make sense of it. He'd never have thought of leaving if his son had decided to stay home. But naturally, wherever his son went, he had to go too.
He stepped up to the desk, where the deed now lay spread out for him to sign. The manager himself handed him the pen and pointed to where he was to write his name.
"Here," he said, "here's where you write your full name—'Hoek Matts Ericsson.'"

As he took the pen, it flashed through his mind how, thirty-one years before, he'd signed a deed acquiring that bit of barren land. He remembered how, after writing his name, he'd gone out to inspect his new property, and how this thought had come to him then: "See what God has given you! Here's work enough to keep you going a lifetime."
The manager, thinking his hesitation was just uncertainty about where to write his name, pointed to the spot again.
"Your name goes there. Now write 'Hoek Matts Ericsson.'"

He put the pen to the paper. "This," he thought, "I write for the sake of my faith and the salvation of my soul, for the sake of my dear friends the Hellgumists, so that I may live with them in unity of spirit, and not be left behind alone when they all go."
And he wrote his first name.

"And this," he thought on, "I write for the sake of my son Gabriel, so I won't lose the dear, good boy who's always been so kind to his old father, and so he can see that, after all, he means more to me than anything else."
And then he wrote his middle name.

"But this," he thought, moving the pen for the third time, "why am I writing this?" Then all at once his hand began to move, as if of its own accord, up and down the page, leaving great black streaks across the hateful document. "This I do because I'm an old man, and I must go on tilling the soil—go on plowing and sowing in the place where I've always worked and slaved."
Hoek Matts Ericsson looked rather sheepish as he turned to the manager and showed him the paper.
"You'll have to excuse me, sir," he said. "It really was my intention to sell the place, but when it came right down to it, I couldn't do it."

chapters.title: Book Three — The Auction
paragraphs: One day in May there was an auction sale at the Ingmar Farm, and what a perfect day it was!--quite as warm as in the summertime. The men had all discarded their long white sheepskin coats and were wearing their short jackets; the women already went about in the loose-sleeved white blouses which belonged with their summer dress.

The schoolmaster's wife was getting ready to attend the auction. Gertrude did not care to go, and Storm was too busy with his class work.
